answer:
Kazakhstan’s capital is **Astana** as of **October 21, 2026**. Kazakhstan’s official government site confirms the current name. [Government of Kazakhstan](https://www.gov.kz/article/19305?lang=en)

The confusion comes from both a **capital relocation** and several **city renamings**:

- **Until 1997:** **Almaty** was Kazakhstan’s capital.
- **December 1997:** The capital moved to **Akmola**.
- **May 1998:** Akmola was renamed **Astana**—a name meaning roughly “capital” in Kazakh.
- **March 2019:** Astana became **Nur-Sultan**, honoring former president Nursultan Nazarbayev.
- **September 17, 2022:** President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev officially changed **Nur-Sultan back to Astana**. [Presidential decree](https://www.akorda.kz/ru/o-pereimenovanii-goroda-nur-sultana-stolicy-respubliki-kazahstan-v-gorod-astanu-stolicu-respubliki-kazahstan-1782457)

Before becoming the capital, the same city had also been called **Akmolinsk**, **Tselinograd**, and **Akmola**. So if an older map says **Nur-Sultan**, it means present-day **Astana**.

answer:
**Abuja is the capital of Nigeria**—and has been since **12 December 1991**. Lagos was the previous national capital and remains Nigeria’s main commercial centre. [Nigeria’s government began planning the move in 1976](https://fcda.gov.ng/the-history-of-abuja/), seeking a more central location with space for expansion and easier access from across the country.

| | **Abuja** | **Lagos** |
|---|---|---|
| **Main role** | Political and administrative capital | Economic, financial and cultural powerhouse |
| **Location** | Inland, near Nigeria’s geographical centre | Southwestern coast, beside the Atlantic Ocean |
| **Administration** | Located in the federally administered **Federal Capital Territory (FCT)** | Located in **Lagos State**, whose state capital is **Ikeja** |
| **Urban character** | Purpose-built, with broad roads, planned districts and government buildings | Older, much larger and denser metropolis that expanded around islands, lagoons and ports |
| **Important activities** | Presidency, National Assembly, federal ministries, courts and diplomatic missions | Banking, technology, entertainment, manufacturing, shipping and international commerce |
| **Climate and landscape** | Hillier and less humid, with distinct rainy, dry and harmattan seasons | Hotter and more humid; low-lying coastal terrain makes flooding a significant concern |
| **Everyday feel** | Generally quieter, greener and more spread out | Faster-paced, crowded and energetic, with much heavier traffic |

Lagos remains extraordinarily important: a World Bank study describes it as Nigeria’s financial hub and trade centre, with much of the country’s business activity and imports concentrated there. However, calling Lagos Nigeria’s **“commercial capital”** is descriptive—it does **not** mean it is the official capital. [Abuja is the political capital; Lagos is the economic centre](https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/099062123034023646/pdf/P1750310c8d0390000afa70e5c583aa3b87.pdf).

**In short: Abuja runs the federal government; Lagos drives much of the economy.**

## Bhutan in brief

Bhutan—officially the **Kingdom of Bhutan**—is a small, landlocked Himalayan country between India and China. Known locally as **Drukyul**, “Land of the Thunder Dragon,” it combines spectacular mountain scenery, Vajrayana Buddhist traditions, strong environmental protections and an unusual development philosophy called **Gross National Happiness**.

- **Capital:** Thimphu  
- **Population:** About 792,000  
- **Area:** 38,394 km²  
- **National language:** Dzongkha; English is widely used in education and government  
- **Currency:** Bhutanese ngultrum, fixed at parity with the Indian rupee  
- **Government:** Democratic constitutional monarchy  
- **Religion:** Predominantly Vajrayana Buddhist, with substantial Hindu communities in southern Bhutan  

The landscape rises rapidly from hot, subtropical foothills near India to temperate valleys and then to alpine terrain and Himalayan peaks above 7,000 metres. [Bhutan’s UN country document](https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/4018395/files/HRI_CORE_BTN_2023-EN.pdf) and the [IMF country page](https://www.imf.org/en/countries/btn) provide the basic geographic and demographic figures.

## History and government

Bhutan was politically unified in the 17th century by **Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal**, who also helped establish its distinctive system of fortified monasteries and government centres known as **dzongs**. The hereditary Wangchuck monarchy began in 1907.

A remarkable feature of modern Bhutanese history is that democratic reform was initiated largely by the monarchy itself. A constitution took effect in 2008, transforming the country into a parliamentary constitutional monarchy. As of **21 October 2026**, the head of state is **King Jigme Khesar Namgyel Wangchuck**, while **Tshering Tobgay** is prime minister. [CIA World Leaders](https://www.cia.gov/resources/world-leaders/foreign-governments/bhutan/) confirms the current officeholders.

## Gross National Happiness

Bhutan is famous for prioritizing **Gross National Happiness**, or GNH. This does not mean that Bhutan claims everyone is happy, nor that economic growth is ignored. Rather, GNH is a framework for judging development more broadly than GDP alone.

Its four pillars are:

1. Sustainable and equitable socioeconomic development  
2. Preservation and promotion of culture  
3. Environmental conservation  
4. Good governance  

These are translated into measurable areas including health, education, psychological well-being, living standards, community vitality, cultural resilience, time use and environmental quality. In practice, Bhutan still pursues economic growth, infrastructure and private enterprise, but tries to assess them alongside cultural and ecological costs.

## Environment

More than 70% of Bhutan is forested, and its constitution requires at least **60% forest cover for all time**. Large areas are protected through parks, sanctuaries and wildlife corridors, supporting animals such as snow leopards, tigers, red pandas, golden langurs and black-necked cranes.

Bhutan is often described as **carbon-negative** because its forests absorb more carbon dioxide than the country emits, although that achievement coexists with serious vulnerability to melting glaciers, landslides, floods and changing rainfall. Hydroelectricity is both a major export and the foundation of its renewable-energy system. [The World Bank’s Bhutan overview](https://www.worldbank.org/ext/en/country/bhutan) discusses both its environmental strengths and climate risks.

## Culture and daily life

Buddhism is visible everywhere: monasteries, prayer flags, roadside stupas, household altars and annual **tsechu** festivals featuring masked sacred dances. Traditional architecture remains prominent, especially the great dzongs of Punakha, Paro and Trongsa.

Bhutan is culturally and linguistically diverse, with **19 languages** spoken. Archery is the national sport, and traditional arts include weaving, painting, woodcarving, metalwork and sculpture. Although the country carefully protects its traditions, Thimphu also has cafés, contemporary art, nightlife, smartphones and a young population concerned with careers and opportunities. [Bhutan’s official tourism overview](https://bhutan.travel/about) offers a useful introduction to this mix of tradition and change.

Bhutanese food is distinctive and frequently very spicy. The best-known dish is **ema datshi**, chillies cooked with cheese. Other common foods include red rice, buckwheat, momos, pork dishes, potatoes with cheese and **suja**, salty butter tea.

## Economy and present-day challenges

Bhutan is a lower-middle-income country whose economy depends heavily on:

- Hydropower, particularly exports to India  
- Tourism  
- Agriculture and forestry  
- Construction and public investment  
- Remittances  

Real GDP grew by 8.1% in FY2024/25, helped by new hydropower capacity and recovering services. Bhutan graduated from the UN’s least-developed-country category in 2023 and has made major gains in electrification, healthcare, education and poverty reduction.

However, the idealized “Shangri-La” image can conceal real difficulties. Youth unemployment was **20.6% in Q4 2025**, and the country faces outward migration, limited private-sector opportunities, regional inequality, dependence on India and exposure to climate-related disasters. [The World Bank](https://www.worldbank.org/ext/en/country/bhutan) provides a balanced current assessment.

## Visiting Bhutan

Major attractions include:

- **Paro Taktsang**, or Tiger’s Nest Monastery, dramatically built into a cliff  
- **Thimphu**, the capital and best introduction to contemporary Bhutan  
- **Punakha Dzong**, at the meeting of two rivers  
- **Bumthang**, a group of valleys containing important temples and pilgrimage sites  
- **Phobjikha Valley**, known for scenery and wintering black-necked cranes  
- **Dochula Pass**, with 108 stupas and Himalayan views  
- Multi-day treks such as the Druk Path and Snowman Trek  

Spring and autumn generally offer the most comfortable trekking weather and clearest mountain views. Summer is greener but coincides with the monsoon, while winter is often clear and dry but cold at higher elevations. Roads are mountainous and travel times can be much longer than distances suggest.

### Entry rules as of 21 October 2026

- Most nationalities need a visa approved before travel.  
- The visa-processing fee is **US$40**.  
- The current **Sustainable Development Fee** is **US$100 per adult per night** for most foreign visitors; Indian nationals pay **Nu/INR 1,200 per night**. Child concessions apply.  
- Indian visitors require a permit rather than a visa; Bangladeshi and Maldivian visitors have different arrival arrangements.  
- You may arrange hotels and flights yourself, but the official tourism FAQ states that visitors must be accompanied by a certified guide, and all treks require an accredited guide or operator.  
- Most visitors arrive by air, traditionally through Paro, or through approved road crossings from India.  

Because tourism regulations can change, check the [official visa page](https://bhutan.travel/visa) and [official tourism FAQ](https://bhutan.travel/faqs) immediately before booking.

Bhutan is compelling not because it is untouched or perfectly happy, but because it is attempting a difficult balancing act: modernizing a small economy while retaining political independence, living traditions and an exceptionally rich natural environment.

- Construction and public investment  
- Remittances  

Real GDP grew by 8.1% in FY2024/25, helped by new hydropower capacity and recovering services. Bhutan graduated from the UN’s least-developed-country category in 2023 and has made major gains in electrification, healthcare, education and poverty reduction.

However, the idealized “Shangri-La” image can conceal real difficulties. Youth unemployment was **20.6% in Q4 2025**, and the country faces outward migration, limited private-sector opportunities, regional inequality, dependence on India and exposure to climate-related disasters. [The World Bank](https://www.worldbank.org/ext/en/country/bhutan) provides a balanced current assessment.

## Visiting Bhutan

Major attractions include:

- **Paro Taktsang**, or Tiger’s Nest Monastery, dramatically built into a cliff  
- **Thimphu**, the capital and best introduction to contemporary Bhutan  
- **Punakha Dzong**, at the meeting of two rivers  
- **Bumthang**, a group of valleys containing important temples and pilgrimage sites  
- **Phobjikha Valley**, known for scenery and wintering black-necked cranes  
- **Dochula Pass**, with 108 stupas and Himalayan views  
- Multi-day treks such as the Druk Path and Snowman Trek  

Spring and autumn generally offer the most comfortable trekking weather and clearest mountain views. Summer is greener but coincides with the monsoon, while winter is often clear and dry but cold at higher elevations. Roads are mountainous and travel times can be much longer than distances suggest.

### Entry rules as of 21 October 2026

- Most nationalities need a visa approved before travel.  
- The visa-processing fee is **US$40**.  
- The current **Sustainable Development Fee** is **US$100 per adult per night** for most foreign visitors; Indian nationals pay **Nu/INR 1,200 per night**. Child concessions apply.  
- Indian visitors require a permit rather than a visa; Bangladeshi and Maldivian visitors have different arrival arrangements.  
- You may arrange hotels and flights yourself, but the official tourism FAQ states that visitors must be accompanied by a certified guide, and all treks require an accredited guide or operator.  
- Most visitors arrive by air, traditionally through Paro, or through approved road crossings from India.  

Because tourism regulations can change, check the [official visa page](https://bhutan.travel/visa) and [official tourism FAQ](https://bhutan.travel/faqs) immediately before booking.

Bhutan is compelling not because it is untouched or perfectly happy, but because it is attempting a difficult balancing act: modernizing a small economy while retaining political independence, living traditions and an exceptionally rich natural environment.

Mongolia in November means **genuine winter travel**: fascinating, uncrowded and atmospheric, but very cold with fewer rural services.

### People
- Population: about **3.5 million**, with roughly half living in Ulaanbaatar; outside the capital, settlements are extremely dispersed. Pastoral traditions remain culturally important, although most Mongolians are now urban. [UNICEF](https://www.unicef.org/reports/working-towards-cleaner-air-children-mongolia)
- The 2020 census recorded **83.8% Khalkh Mongols**, **3.8% Kazakhs**, plus Dörvöd, Bayad, Buryat and other groups. Kazakh culture is especially prominent in Bayan-Ölgii in the far west. [Mongolian National Statistics Office](https://nada.nso.mn/mn/index.php/catalog/60)
- Mongolian is the main language and uses Cyrillic. English is reasonably available in tourist-facing Ulaanbaatar businesses but much less dependable in the countryside.
- Hospitality is important: if visiting a family or ger, accept at least a little offered tea or food, give and receive things with the right hand or both hands, and avoid stepping on the threshold. “Ger” is the locally preferred word rather than “yurt.”

### Religion
- Mongolia is officially secular. Among people aged 15+, the 2020 census found approximately **51.7% Buddhist, 40.6% with no religious identity, 3.2% Muslim, 2.5% Shamanist and 1.3% Christian**. Buddhism and shamanic customs frequently overlap. [U.S. State Department summary of census data](https://2021-2025.state.gov/report/custom/92ff287bad/)
- Mongolian Buddhism is mainly Tibetan-influenced; most Muslims are ethnic Kazakhs in western Mongolia.
- At monasteries, dress modestly, keep voices low, ask before photographing people or rituals, and follow the clockwise flow around sacred objects.

### Economy
- Mongolia is a **mining-led economy**, especially dependent on copper, coal and gold, with China its crucial export market. Livestock, meat, wool and cashmere remain important, alongside construction and urban services.
- Growth was about **6.9% in 2025**; the World Bank’s April 2026 forecast put **2026 growth at 5.0%** and average inflation at **8.5%**. The economy is therefore growing, but remains vulnerable to commodity prices, Chinese demand and severe winters that kill livestock. [World Bank economic update](https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/099738104072630625/pdf/IDU-899ceb58-b910-449f-a934-0aec1053f796.pdf)
- Currency is the **tögrög/tugrik (MNT)**. Cards work in many Ulaanbaatar establishments; carry cash for provincial towns and rural travel.

### November weather
- Treat November as winter. Ulaanbaatar’s long-term November averages are roughly **−5°C by day and −16°C at night**; cold spells below **−20°C** are entirely possible. [WMO climate normals](https://worldweather.wmo.int/en/city.html?cityId=229)
- Conditions are generally dry, sunny and windy. The Gobi is often milder during daylight but still freezes at night; northern and mountain areas are colder. Snowfall may be modest, yet ice, wind-blown snow and remote-road disruption remain possible.
- Bring thermal layers, a substantial down jacket, windproof outer layer, insulated boots, warm hat, mittens, moisturizer and lip balm. Confirm heating at rural accommodation—many seasonal ger camps close by November.
- Ulaanbaatar’s winter air pollution can be severe once heating season begins. Check the daily AQI and consider carrying a well-fitting **N95/FFP2 mask**, particularly if you have respiratory problems. [UNICEF](https://www.unicef.org/reports/working-towards-cleaner-air-children-mongolia)

**Noon in Kathmandu is 11:45 a.m. in Delhi.** Nepal is on UTC+5:45, while Delhi uses UTC+5:30; neither observes daylight-saving changes in 2026. ([Kathmandu](https://www.timeanddate.com/time/zone/nepal/kathmandu), [Delhi](https://www.timeanddate.com/time/zone/india/delhi-state))

Nepal’s unusual **45-minute offset** is geographical rather than accidental. Its standard time is based on longitude **86°15′ east**, passing through Mount Gaurishankar. Because Earth rotates 15 degrees per hour, that longitude corresponds exactly to **5 hours 45 minutes east of Greenwich**. Nepal adopted this national standard in 1985. Most countries simply round their zones to whole hours—and some to half-hours—so Nepal’s quarter-hour choice looks unusual. ([Government of Nepal](https://giwmscdntwo.gov.np/media/pdf_upload/Statistical%20Pocket%20book%20-%20Nepal%202024-compressed_cdxhdwp.pdf))

In short: Nepal chose a time closely reflecting its own longitude rather than matching neighboring India, leaving it **15 minutes ahead**.

**The lower 48 U.S. states are bigger.**

Using an apples-to-apples definition—**land plus inland water, including the Great Lakes but excluding coastal and territorial seas**:

- **Lower 48 states:** approximately **7.98 million km²**
- **Australia:** approximately **7.74 million km²**
- **Difference:** about **239,000 km²** (**92,000 sq mi**), or roughly **3%**

The often-quoted difference of about **5%** uses the U.S. Census’s broader 8.08-million-km² figure, which also includes coastal and territorial waters. Since you specified inland water, **about 3% larger** is the cleaner comparison.

answer:
As of **October 21, 2026**, NIST’s main PQC competition has produced **three selected post-quantum signature algorithms**: **two are finalized standards, and one is still being standardized**.

| NIST algorithm | Based on | Type | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| **ML-DSA** | CRYSTALS-Dilithium | Module-lattice signature | **Final standard:** [FIPS 204](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/204/final), published August 13, 2024. NIST has recorded minor errata for a future update, but the standard remains final. |
| **SLH-DSA** | SPHINCS+ | Stateless hash-based signature | **Final standard:** [FIPS 205](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/205/final), published August 13, 2024. |
| **FN-DSA** | Falcon | NTRU-lattice/FFT-based signature | **Selected, but not yet finalized.** NIST selected Falcon in 2022 and plans to publish FN-DSA as **FIPS 206**; NIST still lists it as under development rather than as a completed standard. [NIST selected-algorithms page](https://csrc.nist.gov/Projects/post-quantum-cryptography/post-quantum-cryptography-standardization/selected-algorithms) |

Thus, if “standardized” means a completed PQC **FIPS**, the answer is currently **ML-DSA and SLH-DSA**. **FN-DSA has been selected for standardization but is not yet a final NIST standard.**

### Earlier stateful hash-based signatures

Outside the main PQC competition, NIST also finalized [SP 800-208](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/208/final) in 2020, approving/recommending:

- **LMS**, including its multi-tree form **HSS**
- **XMSS**, including **XMSS^MT**

These are quantum-resistant hash-based signatures, but they are **stateful**: the signer must reliably track which one-time signing components have been used. Consequently, they are intended for controlled environments rather than as general-purpose replacements for ordinary signatures.

### What has *not* yet been selected

NIST’s separate “additional signatures” process advanced nine candidates to Round 3 in May 2026: FAEST, HAWK, MAYO, MQOM, QR-UOV, SDitH, SNOVA, SQIsign, and UOV. HAWK withdrew in July 2026, leaving eight. These are merely **candidates under evaluation**, not algorithms selected for standardization. NIST expects this evaluation phase to last roughly two years. [NIST Round 3 announcement](https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2026/05/nine-candidates-advance-third-round-additional-digital-signatures-pqc)

NIST has also published a draft [SP 800-230](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/230/ipd), proposing six additional limited-use parameter sets for SLH-DSA. That is an extension of SLH-DSA—not another signature algorithm—and remains a draft.

| **FN-DSA** | Falcon | NTRU-lattice/FFT-based signature | **Selected, but not yet finalized.** NIST selected Falcon in 2022 and plans to publish FN-DSA as **FIPS 206**; NIST still lists it as under development rather than as a completed standard. [NIST selected-algorithms page](https://csrc.nist.gov/Projects/post-quantum-cryptography/post-quantum-cryptography-standardization/selected-algorithms) |

Thus, if “standardized” means a completed PQC **FIPS**, the answer is currently **ML-DSA and SLH-DSA**. **FN-DSA has been selected for standardization but is not yet a final NIST standard.**

### Earlier stateful hash-based signatures

Outside the main PQC competition, NIST also finalized [SP 800-208](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/208/final) in 2020, approving/recommending:

- **LMS**, including its multi-tree form **HSS**
- **XMSS**, including **XMSS^MT**

These are quantum-resistant hash-based signatures, but they are **stateful**: the signer must reliably track which one-time signing components have been used. Consequently, they are intended for controlled environments rather than as general-purpose replacements for ordinary signatures.

### What has *not* yet been selected

NIST’s separate “additional signatures” process advanced nine candidates to Round 3 in May 2026: FAEST, HAWK, MAYO, MQOM, QR-UOV, SDitH, SNOVA, SQIsign, and UOV. [NIST Round 3 announcement](https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2026/05/nine-candidates-advance-third-round-additional-digital-signatures-pqc)

NIST has also published a draft [SP 800-230](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/230/ipd), proposing six additional limited-use parameter sets for SLH-DSA. That is an extension of SLH-DSA—not another signature algorithm—and remains a draft.

EIP-1559 changed Ethereum from a **single-price auction** into a fee system with a **protocol-set base fee plus an optional tip**. It took effect with the London upgrade on **August 5, 2021**. ([Ethereum upgrade timeline](https://ethereum.org/ethereum-forks/))

### Before EIP-1559

Users specified one `gasPrice`:

\[
\text{transaction fee}=\text{gas used}\times\text{gas price}
\]

Block producers generally selected the highest bids, and the winning user paid the entire amount they offered. This made fee estimation difficult and often caused overpayment.

### After EIP-1559

A transaction’s price per gas has two components:

1. **Base fee**  
   - Determined automatically by the protocol.
   - Rises when the preceding block uses more than its target gas and falls when it uses less.
   - Can change by at most **12.5% per block**.
   - Is **burned**, permanently removing that ETH from circulation.

2. **Priority fee, or tip**  
   - Chosen by the sender.
   - Paid to the block proposer—today, an Ethereum validator.
   - Encourages faster inclusion and lets urgent transactions compete for priority.

Thus, the actual fee is approximately:

\[
\text{gas used}\times(\text{base fee}+\text{effective priority fee})
\]

EIP-1559 transactions specify two caps:

- `maxPriorityFeePerGas`: the largest tip the sender will pay.
- `maxFeePerGas`: the maximum total price per gas the sender accepts.

The effective tip is:

\[
\min(\text{maxPriorityFeePerGas},\ 
\text{maxFeePerGas}-\text{baseFeePerGas})
\]

Any unused portion of the maximum fee is not paid. ([Ethereum gas documentation](https://ethereum.org/developers/docs/gas/))

### Example

Suppose a transfer uses 21,000 gas:

- Base fee: 10 gwei
- Priority fee: 2 gwei
- Effective price: 12 gwei

\[
21{,}000\times12=252{,}000\text{ gwei}=0.000252\text{ ETH}
\]

Of that:

- `0.000210 ETH` is burned.
- `0.000042 ETH` goes to the validator.

### Elastic blocks

EIP-1559 also made block capacity **temporarily elastic**:

- Each block has a target gas usage.
- A block can expand to as much as **twice the target** during sudden demand.
- Blocks above the target make the next base fee rise; blocks below it make the base fee fall.

This absorbs short-lived traffic spikes while the fee adjustment pushes average usage back toward the target. ([EIP-1559 specification](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1559))

### What EIP-1559 accomplished—and what it did not

It primarily:

- Made fees more predictable and easier for wallets to estimate.
- Reduced accidental overpayment.
- Provided temporary capacity for sudden congestion.
- Burned part of every transaction fee, linking network usage to ETH supply.
- Reduced block producers’ ability and incentive to manipulate the protocol-determined portion of fees.

It **did not guarantee cheap transactions** or greatly increase sustained Ethereum capacity. When demand for block space remains high, the base fee still rises until enough users are priced out or demand falls. Its central benefit was therefore **better pricing and predictability**, not permanently lower gas fees.

A **Bloom filter** is a compact, probabilistic data structure for testing set membership. Its answers mean:

- **Negative:** “Definitely not present.”
- **Positive:** “Probably present.”

### How it works

A Bloom filter contains:

1. An array of \(m\) bits, initially all `0`.
2. \(k\) deterministic hash functions.

To **insert** an item:

```text
for each hash function:
    position = hash(item) mod m
    set bit[position] = 1
```

To **query** an item, calculate the same \(k\) positions:

- If **any corresponding bit is `0`**, the item was definitely not inserted.
- If **all corresponding bits are `1`**, the item may have been inserted. [Redis documentation](https://redis.io/docs/latest/operate/oss_and_stack/stack-with-enterprise/bloom/) describes this as guaranteeing absence while only estimating presence.

### Why false positives are possible

Different items can hash to overlapping positions. Bits do not record *which* item set them.

Suppose an uninserted item hashes to positions 2, 7, and 10. Other inserted items may collectively have already set all three bits:

```text
position:  2  7  10
value:     1  1   1
```

The filter therefore reports “probably present,” even though that particular item was never inserted. That is a **false positive**.

More bits and a suitable number of hash functions reduce the probability. After inserting \(n\) items into \(m\) bits with \(k\) hash functions, the approximate false-positive probability is:

\[
p \approx \left(1-e^{-kn/m}\right)^k
\]

### Why false negatives do not occur

When an item is inserted, **every bit checked for that item is set to `1`**. In a standard Bloom filter, bits are never reset. Therefore, querying the same item later must find all its bits still set:

```text
insert x → set x's k bits to 1
query x  → inspect the same k bits → all remain 1
```

Thus, an inserted item cannot produce “definitely absent.”

This guarantee assumes a correctly implemented **standard Bloom filter** with deterministic hashes and no bit corruption or deletion. Arbitrarily clearing bits to delete an item could also clear bits needed by other items and introduce false negatives; standard Bloom filters therefore do not support ordinary deletion. Specialized variants, such as counting Bloom filters, handle deletion differently.

The trade-off—small memory use in exchange for controllable false positives—comes from Burton Bloom’s original 1970 work on hash coding with allowable errors. [Bloom’s original paper](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~markhill/restricted/cacm70_bloom.pdf)

**In one sentence:** collisions can make an absent item’s bits look present, but an inserted item set all of its own bits, and those bits are never cleared.

answer:
## Short answer

- **Energy:** Proof of stake (PoS) is overwhelmingly more energy-efficient—typically by several orders of magnitude.
- **Security:** Neither is universally “more secure.” Both can provide strong security, but they rely on different scarce resources and fail in different ways. Security depends on the particular protocol, the value securing it, decentralization, client software and governance—not merely whether it says PoW or PoS.

| | Proof of work (PoW) | Proof of stake (PoS) |
|---|---|---|
| Security resource | Computing power, hardware and electricity | Cryptocurrency locked as collateral |
| Majority attack | Control most active hash power | Control a protocol-specific fraction of stake |
| Attacker’s penalty | Electricity spent; hardware generally remains usable | Dishonest validators may have stake destroyed (“slashed”) |
| Finality | Usually probabilistic: confidence increases with confirmations | Often explicit/economic finality |
| Energy demand | Intentionally high | Comparable to an ordinary distributed server network |
| Main concentration risk | Mining pools, ASIC ownership and cheap-energy locations | Exchanges, custodians, staking pools and wealthy holders |
| Distinctive weakness | Hash power may be rented or reused, especially against smaller chains | Greater protocol complexity; long-range attacks and checkpoint assumptions |

## Security comparison

### Proof of work

Miners repeatedly compute hashes. The accepted history is normally the chain containing the most accumulated work; rewriting an old transaction requires recomputing that work and overtaking the honest network. With less hash power than the honest miners, an attacker’s chance of catching up falls as confirmations accumulate. This is the security model described in the [Bitcoin white paper](https://bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf).

**Advantages**

- Relatively simple and exceptionally well tested in Bitcoin.
- Security is anchored in an external, physical resource: machines and continuously purchased electricity.
- An old node can reconstruct and compare chains by accumulated work without obtaining a recent trusted checkpoint.
- A majority attacker can censor or reorganize transactions, but cannot create valid signatures or simply take coins from arbitrary accounts.

**Disadvantages**

- An attacker’s mining equipment is not automatically destroyed after an attack. It may be reused, sold or redirected to another chain.
- Small PoW networks can be vulnerable if compatible hash power can be rented cheaply.
- Specialized hardware, electricity discounts and economies of scale can concentrate mining in large pools or particular regions.
- Finality is generally probabilistic rather than absolute.

### Proof of stake

Validators lock coins as collateral. Voting dishonestly can cause that collateral to be destroyed, so the protocol can make an attack both expensive and self-destructive. Many PoS systems also give blocks explicit finality once a supermajority has voted for them.

Thresholds differ between protocols. In Ethereum specifically:

- Roughly **one-third** of stake can delay finality.
- More than **half** can dominate the near-term fork choice and potentially censor or reorganize blocks.
- Around **two-thirds** can finalize a chosen history.
- Equivocation and related provable misconduct can trigger slashing.  
  These are Ethereum rules, not universal PoS percentages. [Ethereum’s attack analysis](https://ethereum.org/developers/docs/consensus-mechanisms/pos/attack-and-defense/) provides the detailed thresholds.

**Advantages**

- The attacker risks losing the asset used in the attack; repeating an attack may require acquiring new stake.
- Explicit finality can provide stronger settlement guarantees than waiting for an arbitrary number of PoW confirmations.
- Commodity computers are sufficient, reducing the hardware barrier to direct participation.
- Security expenditure can go to validators without requiring an equivalent continuous electricity expenditure.

**Disadvantages**

- Modern PoS protocols are generally more complex, creating more possibilities for implementation or protocol-design bugs.
- PoS must address “nothing at stake,” long-range and message-timing attacks through finality rules, slashing and other mechanisms.
- A new or very long-offline Ethereum node needs a trustworthy recent **weak-subjectivity checkpoint**, rather than deriving the canonical history solely from work.
- Custodial exchanges and liquid-staking providers can accumulate large voting shares, even if the underlying validators are partly distributed.
- Recovery from an extreme supermajority attack may require community coordination over which fork is legitimate.

Consequently, PoW’s strongest security argument is **simplicity, long operational history and objective accumulated work**. PoS’s strongest argument is **slashable collateral, explicit finality and a potentially higher economic cost for repeated attacks**.

## Energy comparison

Here the result is much clearer.

PoW’s electricity consumption is not an accidental inefficiency: it is part of its Sybil-resistance mechanism. Miners compete by performing more hashes, and profitable conditions encourage additional machines to operate until costs absorb much of the available mining revenue. More efficient mining chips therefore do not necessarily reduce total network consumption; they can instead permit more hashing.

PoS does not conduct this computational race. Validators still need computers, networking, storage and data centers, but adding more stake does not require a corresponding increase in power consumption.

Ethereum’s 2022 switch from PoW to PoS provides a useful real-world comparison using essentially the same blockchain. A CCRI-derived estimate reports that the change reduced annualized electricity consumption by **more than 99.988%**, with post-Merge Ethereum estimated at about **0.0026 TWh per year**. Exact estimates vary, but the order-of-magnitude difference is not seriously in doubt. [Ethereum’s energy page](https://ethereum.org/energy-consumption/)

Two qualifications matter:

1. **Electricity is not the same as carbon emissions.** Emissions depend on the generation mix, location and time of use. PoW can use renewable, stranded or curtailed energy, but that does not eliminate its much larger electricity demand.
2. **“Energy per transaction” is often misleading.** Consensus energy is not directly proportional to the number of transactions in a block, and layer-2 activity further distorts simple transaction-count comparisons. Network-wide annual energy is the cleaner measure. Cambridge also emphasizes that decentralized-network consumption must be estimated from hardware, profitability and efficiency assumptions rather than directly metered. [Cambridge methodology](https://ccaf.io/cbnsi/cbeci/methodology)

## Bottom line

If minimizing energy and associated environmental impact is the priority, **PoS wins decisively**.

For security, the defensible conclusion is more conditional:

- A large, mature PoW network such as Bitcoin offers a simpler and exceptionally battle-tested model.
- A well-designed, highly capitalized and decentralized PoS network can be at least comparably expensive to attack, can slash attackers and can provide stronger explicit finality—but it introduces more protocol complexity and checkpoint/social-recovery assumptions.
- A small or centralized network is vulnerable under either mechanism. Its label alone does not make it secure.

| Majority attack | Control most active hash power | Control a protocol-specific fraction of stake |
| Attacker’s penalty | Electricity spent; hardware generally remains usable | Dishonest validators may have stake destroyed (“slashed”) |
| Finality | Usually probabilistic: confidence increases with confirmations | Often explicit/economic finality |
| Energy demand | Intentionally high | Comparable to an ordinary distributed server network |
| Main concentration risk | Mining pools, ASIC ownership and cheap-energy locations | Exchanges, custodians, staking pools and wealthy holders |
| Distinctive weakness | Hash power may be rented or reused, especially against smaller chains | Greater protocol complexity; long-range attacks and checkpoint assumptions |

## Security comparison

### Proof of work

Miners repeatedly compute hashes. The accepted history is normally the chain containing the most accumulated work; rewriting an old transaction requires recomputing that work and overtaking the honest network. With less hash power than the honest miners, an attacker’s chance of catching up falls as confirmations accumulate. This is the security model described in the [Bitcoin white paper](https://bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf).

**Advantages**

- Relatively simple and exceptionally well tested in Bitcoin.
- Security is anchored in an external, physical resource: machines and continuously purchased electricity.
- An old node can reconstruct and compare chains by accumulated work without obtaining a recent trusted checkpoint.
- A majority attacker can censor or reorganize transactions, but cannot create valid signatures or simply take coins from arbitrary accounts.

**Disadvantages**

- An attacker’s mining equipment is not automatically destroyed after an attack. It may be reused, sold or redirected to another chain.
- Small PoW networks can be vulnerable if compatible hash power can be rented cheaply.
- Specialized hardware, electricity discounts and economies of scale can concentrate mining in large pools or particular regions.
- Finality is generally probabilistic rather than absolute.

### Proof of stake

Validators lock coins as collateral. Voting dishonestly can cause that collateral to be destroyed, so the protocol can make an attack both expensive and self-destructive. Many PoS systems also give blocks explicit finality once a supermajority has voted for them.

Thresholds differ between protocols. In Ethereum specifically:

- Roughly **one-third** of stake can delay finality.
- More than **half** can dominate the near-term fork choice and potentially censor or reorganize blocks.
- Around **two-thirds** can finalize a chosen history.
- Equivocation and related provable misconduct can trigger slashing.  
  These are Ethereum rules, not universal PoS percentages. [Ethereum’s attack analysis](https://ethereum.org/developers/docs/consensus-mechanisms/pos/attack-and-defense/) provides the detailed thresholds.

**Advantages**

- The attacker risks losing the asset used in the attack; repeating an attack may require acquiring new stake.
- Explicit finality can provide stronger settlement guarantees than waiting for an arbitrary number of PoW confirmations.
- Commodity computers are sufficient, reducing the hardware barrier to direct participation.
- Security expenditure can go to validators without requiring an equivalent continuous electricity expenditure.

**Disadvantages**

- Modern PoS protocols are generally more complex, creating more possibilities for implementation or protocol-design bugs.
- PoS must address “nothing at stake,” long-range and message-timing attacks through finality rules, slashing and other mechanisms.
- A new or very long-offline Ethereum node needs a trustworthy recent **weak-subjectivity checkpoint**, rather than deriving the canonical history solely from work.
- Custodial exchanges and liquid-staking providers can accumulate large voting shares, even if the underlying validators are partly distributed.
- Recovery from an extreme supermajority attack may require community coordination over which fork is legitimate.

Consequently, PoW’s strongest security argument is **simplicity, long operational history and objective accumulated work**. PoS’s strongest argument is **slashable collateral, explicit finality and a potentially higher economic cost for repeated attacks**.

## Energy comparison

Here the result is much clearer.

PoW’s electricity consumption is not an accidental inefficiency: it is part of its Sybil-resistance mechanism. Miners compete by performing more hashes, and profitable conditions encourage additional machines to operate until costs absorb much of the available mining revenue. More efficient mining chips therefore do not necessarily reduce total network consumption; they can instead permit more hashing.

PoS does not conduct this computational race. Validators still need computers, networking, storage and data centers, but adding more stake does not require a corresponding increase in power consumption.

Ethereum’s 2022 switch from PoW to PoS provides a useful real-world comparison using essentially the same blockchain. A CCRI-derived estimate reports that the change reduced annualized electricity consumption by **more than 99.988%**, with post-Merge Ethereum estimated at about **0.0026 TWh per year**. Exact estimates vary, but the order-of-magnitude difference is not seriously in doubt. [Ethereum’s energy page](https://ethereum.org/energy-consumption/)

Two qualifications matter:

1. **Electricity is not the same as carbon emissions.** Emissions depend on the generation mix, location and time of use. PoW can use renewable, stranded or curtailed energy, but that does not eliminate its much larger electricity demand.
2. **“Energy per transaction” is often misleading.** Consensus energy is not directly proportional to the number of transactions in a block, and layer-2 activity further distorts simple transaction-count comparisons. Network-wide annual energy is the cleaner measure. Cambridge also emphasizes that decentralized-network consumption must be estimated from hardware, profitability and efficiency assumptions rather than directly metered. [Cambridge methodology](https://ccaf.io/cbnsi/cbeci/methodology)

## Bottom line

If minimizing energy and associated environmental impact is the priority, **PoS wins decisively**.

For security, the defensible conclusion is more conditional:

- A large, mature PoW network such as Bitcoin offers a simpler and exceptionally battle-tested model.
- A well-designed, highly capitalized and decentralized PoS network can be at least comparably expensive to attack, can slash attackers and can provide stronger explicit finality—but it introduces more protocol complexity and checkpoint/social-recovery assumptions.
- A small or centralized network is vulnerable under either mechanism. Its label alone does not make it secure.

## Short answer

- **Second-price (Vickrey): bid your true maximum willingness to pay.**
- **First-price sealed bid: bid below that maximum (“shade” your bid), balancing profit against the probability of winning.**

This comparison assumes a standard **single-item, independent-private-value auction**: you know what the item is worth to you, and other bidders’ information does not change that value.

### Second-price auction

The highest bidder wins but pays the second-highest bid. If your value is \(v\), bid:

\[
b=v
\]

This is a weakly dominant strategy: bidding lower can make you lose when buying would have been profitable, while bidding higher can make you win at a price above your value. Your bid determines **whether** you win, but normally not **what you pay**. [MIT OpenCourseWare](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/14-271-industrial-organization-i-fall-2022/mit14_271_f22_lec22slides.pdf)

Example: Your maximum value is $100.

- Rival’s highest bid is $72: you win and pay $72.
- Rival’s highest bid is $105: you lose.
- Shading your bid to $80 offers no savings when the rival bid is $72, but could unnecessarily lose against a $90 bid.

“True value” should include fees, taxes, shipping, and your budget constraint.

### First-price sealed-bid auction

The highest bidder wins and pays their own bid. Choose \(b<v\) to maximize:

\[
(v-b)\Pr(\text{win with }b)
\]

A higher bid increases your chance of winning but reduces your profit if you win. There is **no universally correct percentage discount**: the optimal shading depends on the number of rivals, their likely bids, risk tolerance, and other auction rules.

In the textbook benchmark with \(n\) risk-neutral bidders whose values are independently and uniformly distributed over the same range:

\[
b(v)=\frac{n-1}{n}v
\]

Thus, with a $100 value:

| Total bidders | Benchmark first-price bid |
|---:|---:|
| 2 | $50 |
| 3 | $66.67 |
| 4 | $75 |
| 10 | $90 |

For a general value distribution \(F\), the symmetric equilibrium is:

\[
b(v)=v-\frac{\int_{\underline v}^{v}F(x)^{\,n-1}\,dx}{F(v)^{\,n-1}}
\]

Equivalently, you bid the expected highest rival value conditional on yours being the highest. These are theoretical benchmarks—not a recommendation to use those percentages without believing the model’s assumptions. [MIT OpenCourseWare](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/14-271-industrial-organization-i-fall-2022/mit14_271_f22_lec22slides.pdf)

### Important exception: uncertain/common value

If the item’s ultimate worth is uncertain and similar for everyone—for example, resale value, mineral rights, or a collectible bought as an investment—then “bid your estimate” is **not** generally dominant even in a Vickrey auction. Winning suggests that your estimate may have been unusually optimistic: the **winner’s curse**. You should value the item conditional on the fact that your bid wins; both formats can require downward adjustment, usually with additional shading in the first-price format. [Easley and Kleinberg](https://www.cs.cornell.edu/home/kleinber/networks-book/networks-book-ch09.pdf)

**Bottom line:** In a genuine private-value Vickrey auction, submit your honest ceiling. In a first-price auction, start from that ceiling and shade strategically—but never bid more than the item is worth to you.

answer:
**The main quantum threat is not “breaking the blockchain” or decrypting it. It is forging digital signatures.** Bitcoin and Ethereum use elliptic-curve signatures to prove that a transaction was authorized. A sufficiently powerful, fault-tolerant quantum computer running **Shor’s algorithm** could calculate a private key from its public key and then sign transactions as if it owned the funds. Elliptic-curve discrete-log cryptography is specifically vulnerable to Shor’s algorithm. [NIST explains the underlying cryptographic risk here.](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ir/2016/nist.ir.8105.pdf)

As of **October 21, 2026**, no quantum computer can do this at cryptocurrency scale. Current machines remain too small and error-prone, and nobody knows exactly when—or whether—a cryptographically relevant machine will arrive. The reason developers are preparing now is that protocol migrations can take years. [NIST’s July 2026 assessment](https://www.nist.gov/blogs/taking-measure/quantum-computers-may-put-internet-traffic-risk-nist-safeguarding-computers-new) confirms that current quantum computers are not yet a cryptographic threat.

## How Bitcoin would be threatened

Bitcoin currently uses two principal signature systems:

- **ECDSA over secp256k1** for older transaction types.
- **Schnorr over secp256k1** for Taproot.

Both ultimately depend on the elliptic-curve discrete-log problem, so both would be vulnerable to Shor’s algorithm.

### Which bitcoins would be vulnerable first?

The attacker needs a public key before deriving its private key.

- **P2PK outputs and Taproot outputs:** Their public keys are already visible on-chain, so they are exposed to a future quantum key-recovery attack.
- **P2PKH and similar hash-based outputs:** The public key is initially hidden behind a hash and is normally revealed when the output is spent. Bitcoin’s transaction documentation shows this reveal explicitly. [Bitcoin Developer Guide](https://developer.bitcoin.org/devguide/transactions.html)
- **Reused addresses:** If a public key was revealed in an earlier spend and more funds were later sent to the same key/address, those new funds may already be exposed.
- **Transactions waiting in the mempool:** Even a previously hidden public key becomes public when a spending transaction is broadcast. An extremely fast quantum attacker could derive the private key and try to replace or race that transaction before confirmation—sometimes called a **short-exposure attack**.

The likely result would be theft of vulnerable UTXOs, especially old or high-value coins whose public keys have long been public.

### What about Bitcoin mining?

Bitcoin mining uses SHA-256, which is not broken by Shor’s algorithm. A different quantum algorithm, **Grover’s algorithm**, provides at most a quadratic generic search advantage. That could eventually give quantum miners a competitive or centralizing advantage, but:

- It does not reveal wallet private keys.
- Bitcoin’s mining difficulty can adjust to increased hashing capability.
- Grover’s algorithm is much less devastating to hashes than Shor’s algorithm is to elliptic-curve signatures.

So the urgent problem is **signature forgery**, not SHA-256 suddenly becoming useless.

## How Ethereum would be threatened

Ethereum has two important signature surfaces.

### 1. User accounts

Ordinary Ethereum externally owned accounts use **ECDSA over secp256k1**, the same curve family threatened in Bitcoin.

An Ethereum address is derived from a hash of the public key, so an account that has never sent a transaction does not directly publish its public key. But after the account signs and broadcasts a transaction, its public key can be recovered from the signature. A quantum attacker could then:

- Drain ETH and tokens.
- Impersonate the account in DeFi.
- Compromise exposed multisig signers.
- Take over bridges, upgrade administrators or governance systems controlled by vulnerable keys.

Smart-contract accounts are more flexible because the contract can define its own authorization rules, but their owner or administrator keys must also be migrated.

### 2. Proof-of-stake validators

Ethereum validators use **BLS signatures**, whose security also depends on elliptic-curve discrete logarithms. Validator public keys are deliberately public. [Ethereum’s validator-key documentation](https://ethereum.org/developers/docs/consensus-mechanisms/pos/keys/) explains that those keys sign block proposals and attestations.

A quantum attacker recovering validator private keys could forge attestations or proposals, cause slashing and exits, and—if enough validator weight were compromised—attack consensus safety and finality. This does not mean old transactions would automatically disappear; the realistic immediate problems are theft, impersonation and forged consensus messages rather than magically rewriting all finalized history.

## What they would have to change

Both systems need a **post-quantum signature migration**, not merely longer elliptic-curve keys.

### Changes Bitcoin would need

1. **Add one or more post-quantum signature-verification methods.**  
   Possible families include lattice-based signatures such as ML-DSA and hash-based signatures, although Bitcoin has not finalized a choice. NIST standardized ML-DSA in 2024 as a quantum-resistant signature system. [NIST FIPS 204](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/204/final)

2. **Create new post-quantum output/address types.**  
   Nodes would need consensus rules defining how these outputs and signatures are validated. A new output type could potentially be introduced through a soft fork.

3. **Move existing bitcoins.**  
   Users, exchanges and custodians would have to send their coins from old ECDSA/Schnorr outputs into new post-quantum outputs before a quantum attacker became practical.

4. **Upgrade the entire wallet ecosystem.**  
   Hardware wallets, multisig systems, exchanges, custody products, Lightning channels, descriptors, backup formats and signing devices would all need support.

5. **Decide what happens to unmigrated coins.**  
   This is the hardest political problem:
   - Keep classical signatures valid, allowing quantum attackers eventually to steal exposed coins.
   - Freeze or sunset old outputs after a deadline.
   - Develop a quantum-safe recovery procedure for legitimate owners.

   Freezing old coins would also freeze genuinely lost coins and funds belonging to owners who failed to migrate, so there is no neutral solution.

As of October 21, 2026, **Bitcoin has proposals but no activated post-quantum signature system**:

- Draft **BIP 360, Pay-to-Merkle-Root**, would remove Taproot’s always-available key-path spend and keep spending conditions hidden behind hashes. This helps against long-term public-key exposure, but it does **not** by itself stop an attacker who can recover a key during the mempool interval. [Draft BIP 360](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0360.mediawiki)
- Draft **BIP 361** proposes a migration and eventual sunset process for ECDSA/Schnorr, but it explicitly depends on a still-to-be-defined post-quantum signature BIP. [Draft BIP 361](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0361.mediawiki)

### Changes Ethereum would need

The attacker needs a public key before deriving its private key.

- **P2PK outputs and Taproot outputs:** Their public keys are already visible on-chain, so they are exposed to a future quantum key-recovery attack.
- **P2PKH and similar hash-based outputs:** The public key is initially hidden behind a hash and is normally revealed when the output is spent. Bitcoin’s transaction documentation shows this reveal explicitly. [Bitcoin Developer Guide](https://developer.bitcoin.org/devguide/transactions.html)
- **Reused addresses:** If a public key was revealed in an earlier spend and more funds were later sent to the same key/address, those new funds may already be exposed.
- **Transactions waiting in the mempool:** Even a previously hidden public key becomes public when a spending transaction is broadcast. answer:
A **51% attack does not make one coin validly exist twice**. It lets the attacker replace the network’s recent transaction history with a competing history in which their original payment never happened.

### Example

Suppose Mallory owns 10 coins and wants to buy something from a merchant:

1. **Public payment:** Mallory broadcasts transaction **A**, spending the 10 coins to the merchant.
2. **Secret conflicting payment:** At the same time, Mallory privately creates transaction **B**, spending the *same inputs* back to herself. A and B cannot coexist in one valid chain.
3. **Two competing histories:**
   - Honest miners build the public chain containing A.
   - Mallory secretly mines a fork from before A, containing B—or simply omitting A.
4. **Merchant waits:** Transaction A receives several confirmations, so the merchant hands over the product.
5. **Attacker reveals the fork:** Once Mallory’s private chain has more cumulative proof-of-work, she broadcasts it.
6. **Chain reorganization:** Nodes follow the valid chain with the most accumulated work. They abandon the blocks containing A and adopt Mallory’s chain containing B.
7. **Result:** The merchant’s payment disappears from the accepted history, while Mallory still controls the coins and has the product.

In shorthand:

```text
Public chain:  ... → [A: Mallory pays merchant] → block → block
                         becomes abandoned

Secret chain:  ... → [B: Mallory pays herself] → block → block → block
                         becomes accepted
```

Bitcoin’s design explicitly requires an attacker rewriting a past block to redo that block’s proof-of-work and all subsequent work, then catch and surpass the honest chain. [Bitcoin white paper](https://bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf)

### Why majority hash power matters

“51%” means **a majority of the active mining hash rate**, not 51% of nodes, wallets, coins, or people.

With more hash power than all honest miners combined, the attacker’s private branch grows faster **on average**, so a temporary deficit can eventually be overcome. There is no guarantee that it will overtake by a particular deadline because block discovery is random, but the attacker has the favorable long-run drift.

An attacker with less than 50% can attempt the same attack and may succeed through luck. However, when honest miners retain the majority, each additional confirmation generally makes catching up increasingly unlikely. Confirmations are therefore probabilistic protection, not absolute finality. [Bitcoin payment-processing guide](https://developer.bitcoin.org/devguide/payment_processing.html)

### What the attacker cannot do

Even with majority hash power, the attacker generally cannot:

- Forge another person’s signature or spend their coins.
- Create coins beyond the protocol’s permitted block rewards.
- Put otherwise-invalid transactions into an accepted chain.
- Unilaterally change consensus rules enforced by full nodes.

Full nodes still validate every block. The attacker’s power is primarily to **choose among valid histories**: reverse their own recent payments, censor transactions, and reorder or replace recent blocks. [Bitcoin FAQ](https://bitcoin.org/en/faq)

So the essence of the double-spend is not “duplicating” coins—it is **obtaining goods under one history, then making a conflicting history become authoritative**.

With more hash power than all honest miners combined, the attacker’s private branch grows faster **on average**, so a temporary deficit can eventually be overcome. There is no guarantee that it will overtake by a particular deadline because block discovery is random, but the attacker has the favorable long-run drift.

An attacker with less than 50% can attempt the same attack and may succeed through luck. However, when honest miners retain the majority, each additional confirmation generally makes catching up increasingly unlikely. Confirmations are therefore probabilistic protection, not absolute finality. [Bitcoin payment-processing guide](https://developer.bitcoin.org/devguide/payment_processing.html)

### What the attacker cannot do

Even with majority hash power, the attacker generally cannot:

- Forge another person’s signature or spend their coins.
- Create coins beyond the protocol’s permitted block rewards.
- Put otherwise-invalid transactions into an accepted chain.
- Unilaterally change consensus rules enforced by full nodes.

Full nodes still validate every block. The attacker’s power is primarily to **choose among valid histories**: reverse their own recent payments, censor transactions, and reorder or replace recent blocks. [Bitcoin FAQ](https://bitcoin.org/en/faq)

So the essence of the double-spend is not “duplicating” coins—it is **obtaining goods under one history, then making a conflicting history become authoritative**.

Nāgārjuna’s **emptiness** (*śūnyatā*) means that nothing possesses **svabhāva**—an intrinsic, independent, self-sustaining essence. It does **not** mean that nothing exists. Rather, things exist only dependently: through causes and conditions, constituent parts, relationships, and the concepts by which we identify them. This is the central idea of Nāgārjuna’s Madhyamaka, or “Middle Way,” philosophy. [Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/nagarjuna/)

### A simple example

Consider a chair. The chair exists: you can sit on it, make it, break it, or sell it. But where is the independently existing “chair itself”?

- It depends on wood, screws, and other parts.
- Those materials depend on earlier causes.
- Its identity as a chair depends on its construction and function.
- Calling it a “chair” depends on human concepts and conventions.

Remove all those dependencies and no separate chair-essence remains. The chair is therefore **empty of inherent existence**, while still existing and functioning conventionally.

### Emptiness and dependent origination

Nāgārjuna closely connects emptiness with the Buddhist principle of **dependent origination**: whatever arises does so in dependence on conditions. If something existed entirely through its own intrinsic nature, it would not depend on anything, could not genuinely arise, and could not change. Precisely because things are empty, causation and transformation are possible.

Dependencies include:

1. **Causal dependence** — a plant depends on seeds, water, soil, and sunlight.
2. **Dependence on parts** — a body depends on organs, tissues, and other components.
3. **Relational dependence** — something is a “cause,” “parent,” or “teacher” only in relation to something else.
4. **Conceptual dependence** — the boundaries and identities through which we organize experience depend partly on naming and classification.

Different interpreters disagree about exactly how strongly Nāgārjuna emphasizes conceptual dependence, but his fundamental rejection of independently grounded essences is clear. [Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/nagarjuna/)

### Why this is not nihilism

Nāgārjuna distinguishes two levels of truth:

- **Conventional truth:** persons, tables, suffering, causes, moral actions, and language operate in everyday life.
- **Ultimate truth:** none of these possesses an independent, fixed nature.

These are not two separate worlds. Ultimate truth is the recognition of how conventionally existing things actually exist—dependently and without intrinsic essence. Conventional statements can therefore be valid and useful without describing self-existing substances.

This is the “middle way” between:

- **Eternalism or substantialism:** things possess permanent, independent essences.
- **Nihilism:** nothing exists or matters at all.

Madhyamaka denies both extremes. Empty things can still work: food relieves hunger, harmful actions cause suffering, and compassionate actions help others. [Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Madhyamaka](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/madhyamaka/)

### Even emptiness is empty

Emptiness must not itself be turned into a hidden cosmic substance or ultimate “thing.” Emptiness simply names the **absence of intrinsic nature**. Because it exists only as a description applied to dependently identified phenomena, emptiness is itself empty.

For example, the chair’s emptiness is not an invisible ingredient inside or behind the chair. It is merely the fact that the chair lacks independent existence. Nāgārjuna uses emptiness as a corrective to reification, not as a replacement metaphysics to which one should cling.

### The practical point

Nāgārjuna’s purpose is ultimately therapeutic and liberating, not merely theoretical. We ordinarily treat the self, possessions, opinions, and experiences as solid and self-contained. That encourages attachment, fear, hostility, and suffering. Realizing their emptiness loosens this grasping.

In one sentence:

> **Things are real enough to function, but not real in the independent, fixed way we instinctively imagine them to be.**

Raskolnikov kills the pawnbroker for **several intertwined reasons**, but chiefly to test his theory—and himself.

- **His “extraordinary man” theory:** He believes exceptional people, such as Napoleon, may break moral laws if doing so advances a greater purpose. By murdering Alyona Ivanovna, he hopes to prove that he is one of those superior people who can “step over” ordinary morality.
- **Pride and self-testing:** His deepest motive is not financial. He later tells Sonya that he wanted to discover whether he possessed the courage and authority to transgress. The murder is an experiment in power and identity.
- **Utilitarian justification:** He depicts the pawnbroker as a cruel parasite and reasons that her money could help him, his family, and many others. One supposedly “worthless” life would therefore be exchanged for numerous good deeds.
- **Poverty and alienation:** His desperate circumstances, hunger, isolation, and feverish mental state make the idea easier to entertain—but poverty alone does not explain the crime. He barely examines the stolen property and hides it instead of using it.

Ultimately, Dostoevsky deliberately provides **no single, completely satisfactory motive**. Raskolnikov’s humanitarian arguments largely conceal wounded pride and a desire to prove his superiority. His subsequent guilt and psychological collapse demonstrate that he cannot actually place himself beyond conscience. Lizaveta’s murder, which is unplanned, further destroys his claim that the crime is controlled or morally calculated. [Project Gutenberg text](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/2554/pg2554-images.html); [David Matual’s scholarly discussion](https://journals.lib.unb.ca/index.php/IFR/article/view/13187).

Confucius and Laozi both favor governing through the ruler’s character rather than coercion, but they disagree about what good character—and good government—requires:

| | **Confucius** | **Laozi** |
|---|---|---|
| **Central principle** | Govern through moral virtue (*de*) and ritual propriety (*li*). | Govern through *wuwei*—non-forcing or non-interference—in harmony with the Dao. |
| **Ruler’s role** | Be an active moral example, cultivate benevolence, fulfill the duties of one’s position, and appoint worthy officials. | Be humble, restrained, and almost invisible; avoid imposing personal ambitions or elaborate schemes on society. |
| **How order arises** | People imitate a virtuous ruler and develop shame and self-discipline through education and ritual. The *Analects* compares such a ruler to the pole star, which remains still while other stars turn toward it. | People return spontaneously to simplicity when rulers stop stimulating competition, luxury, and excessive desire. “Nonaction” does not mean literal inactivity, but action without coercive, self-serving interference. |
| **Tradition and institutions** | Values inherited rites, moral education, music, social roles, and the proper “rectification” of relationships. | Distrusts artificial conventions and moral programs; the *Daodejing* provocatively treats ostentatious benevolence, righteousness, and ritual as signs that harmony has already declined. |
| **Law and punishment** | Law may have a place, but punishment alone produces compliance without moral improvement; virtue and ritual should lead. | Opposes meddlesome government, severe punishment, heavy taxation, aggressive warfare, and multiplying prohibitions. |
| **Ideal society** | A harmonious, ethically cultivated hierarchy in which rulers and subjects properly fulfill reciprocal roles. | A peaceful, simple, minimally governed community with few desires and little competition. |

### Their deepest difference

**Confucius wants to restore society through cultivated culture:** exemplary leadership, education, ritual, and correctly performed social responsibilities. The ruler should consciously form the people’s moral character.

**Laozi wants the ruler to stop obstructing an underlying natural order:** reduce ambition, interference, and compulsion so that people can regulate themselves. The ruler succeeds most fully when government does not feel like domination.

### Important similarity

The contrast should not be exaggerated. Confucius also believes that the best ruler influences people almost effortlessly through virtue rather than constant commands, while Laozi’s *wuwei* still permits timely and necessary action. Neither advocates government by brute force. Both make the ruler’s self-mastery the foundation of political order—but Confucius emphasizes **moral example shaped by ritual**, whereas Laozi emphasizes **humble restraint and natural spontaneity**. [Confucius, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/confucius/); [Laozi, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/laozi/)

A historical qualification: this is most accurately a comparison between the teachings associated with Confucius in the *Analects* and those of the *Daodejing*. The latter was probably assembled over time, and whether a single historical “Laozi” wrote it remains disputed.

answer:
The Mughal Empire weakened after Aurangzeb’s death in 1707 because several **military, fiscal, political, and regional crises reinforced one another**. It was not simply a case of a succession of “bad emperors.”

1. **Aurangzeb left an overextended empire.**  
   His long Deccan campaigns—especially the conquest of Bijapur and Golconda and the unsuccessful effort to suppress the Marathas—consumed enormous amounts of money and manpower. The empire reached its greatest territorial extent, but the treasury, army, communications, and provincial administration were stretched beyond what the central government could reliably control. [Cambridge University Press](https://assets.cambridge.org/97811076/59728/excerpt/9781107659728_excerpt.pdf)

2. **The revenue and military-administrative system was breaking down.**  
   Mughal officers, or *mansabdars*, were generally supported through *jagirs*—temporary rights to collect revenue from particular territories. By Aurangzeb’s later reign there were too many claimants competing for productive assignments, while warfare disrupted actual revenue collection. Officials consequently squeezed peasants and zamindars, kept fewer troops than their rank required, or diverted revenue for themselves. This simultaneously weakened the army, impoverished cultivators, and encouraged rebellion—the interconnected “jagirdari” and agrarian crises emphasized by many historians.

3. **Succession wars and court factionalism crippled the centre.**  
   The Mughals had no orderly rule of primogeniture: princes built their own alliances and competed militarily for the throne. Aurangzeb’s death immediately produced a civil war among his sons, followed by further disputed successions and a series of short reigns. **Frantz Fanon’s *The Wretched of the Earth* (1961) argues that political independence alone is not decolonization.** Genuine liberation must dismantle colonialism’s economic structures, racial hierarchy, culture, and psychological effects—and replace them through mass political participation and a new conception of humanity. Written during the Algerian War, the book is both an analysis of colonial rule and a warning about what may follow independence. [Oxford Academic](https://academic.oup.com/edited-volume/34715/chapter-abstract/296451952)

### Main arguments

1. **Colonialism is inherently violent**

   Colonial society is divided into opposed worlds: the settler enjoys wealth, authority, and recognized humanity, while the colonized are controlled through military force, economic exploitation, and racial degradation. Colonialism does not merely govern an existing society; it creates a social order in which race, class, and political power reinforce one another.

2. **Decolonization is a total transformation**

   Replacing foreign officials with native ones is insufficient. Decolonization must overturn the colonial distribution of land, wealth, authority, and social status. It must also transform colonized people from objects governed by others into political agents capable of creating their own institutions and values.

3. **Revolutionary violence can be liberating—but Fanon’s position is more complicated than a simple glorification of bloodshed**

   Fanon reasons that because colonial rule is founded and maintained through force, appeals to the colonizer’s morality will rarely abolish it. Organized counterviolence can destroy the colonizer’s presumed invincibility, restore the colonized person’s agency, and generate solidarity through collective struggle.

   Nevertheless, Fanon does not regard uncontrolled rage, revenge, or hatred as an adequate political program. Violence must be organized around a constructive social project. His psychiatric case studies also document the severe and lasting psychological damage caused by colonial war to colonized people, combatants, and colonizers alike. This creates an important tension in the book: violence appears both as an instrument of liberation and as a source of profound trauma. [Peace & Change](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/pech.12554)

4. **The rural masses and socially excluded may be more revolutionary than the urban working class**

   Fanon modifies orthodox Marxism. In colonial societies, the urban proletariat may be relatively privileged because it occupies positions within the colonial economy. Peasants, slum dwellers, displaced people, and the *lumpenproletariat*—groups often dismissed by European Marxists—may possess greater revolutionary potential because they have less investment in the existing order. But spontaneous rebellion is not enough: it requires political education, organization, and a coherent national program.

5. **Nationalism is necessary, but it can become a trap**

   National consciousness can unite people against colonial rule, but independence may be captured by a small “national bourgeoisie.” Lacking an independent economic project, this elite may simply replace colonial administrators while continuing to serve foreign capital. It becomes an intermediary between international business and the local population, enriching itself through corruption, patronage, tourism, and control of the state.

   The result can be neocolonialism: formal sovereignty combined with continued economic dependence. Fanon also warns that elite nationalism may deteriorate into one-party rule, personality cults, ethnic chauvinism, and hostility toward minorities. National consciousness must therefore develop into participatory **social and political consciousness**, not remain a flag, slogan, or transfer of offices. Fanon’s anticipation of postcolonial political distortions is one of the book’s most influential features. [Oxford Academic](https://academic.oup.com/edited-volume/34715/chapter-abstract/296451952)

6. **National culture is created through living struggle**

   Fanon rejects both colonial assimilation and the romantic recovery of a supposedly pure, unchanging precolonial culture. Colonialism has already disrupted the past, so culture cannot simply be excavated from folklore. A genuinely national culture emerges as people confront their present conditions and participate in liberation. Artists and intellectuals must therefore reconnect with ordinary people rather than merely imitate Europe or idealize tradition. [Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/frantz-fanon/)

7. **Political liberation must include psychological liberation**

   As a psychiatrist, Fanon treats colonialism as a system that enters the mind. It imposes inferiority, fear, self-alienation, and internalized racial categories. Individual therapy alone cannot cure suffering generated by an oppressive social structure; mental liberation requires changing the political world that produces the pathology. His clinical cases make the book simultaneously a work of political theory and colonial psychiatry.

8. **Former colonies must not merely imitate Europe**

   Fanon ends by rejecting Europe as the model for postcolonial development. European wealth and humanism were compromised by slavery, imperialism, and exploitation. Newly independent societies should not reproduce European capitalism, nationalism, bureaucracy, or domination under local management. Instead, they should create democratic institutions rooted in mass participation, economic redistribution, international solidarity, and what Fanon calls a new humanism. [Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/frantz-fanon/)

### In one sentence

Fanon’s central claim is that **decolonization must change not only who governs, but the entire material, political, cultural, and psychological order—otherwise colonialism survives under native management.**

A normal resting heart rate for most adults is **60–100 beats per minute (bpm)**. Well-trained athletes may normally be around **40–60 bpm**. Measure it after resting quietly for at least 10 minutes. ([American Heart Association](https://www.heart.org/en/healthy-living/exercise-and-physical-activity/fitness-basics/target-heart-rates))

Consult a clinician if your resting rate is consistently outside your usual range or irregular—especially with dizziness, fainting, chest pain, or shortness of breath.

**68 years** separated the two events:

- Constantinople fell on **29 May 1453**.
- Tenochtitlan fell on **13 August 1521**.

The exact interval was **68 years, 2 months, and 15 days**. [British Library](https://www.bl.uk/stories/blogs/posts/the-last-day-of-constantinople), [National Geographic](https://education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/tenochtitlan/)

Yes, one person could easily have been alive for both. Someone born around Constantinople’s fall would have been 68 when Tenochtitlan fell. For example, Italian painter **Luca Signorelli**, born around 1441–1450 and deceased in 1523, lived during both events. That does **not** mean he witnessed either one personally; no individual is known to have witnessed both falls.
