## Moldova in brief

**Moldova is a small, landlocked country between Romania and Ukraine.** It combines a Romanian-speaking cultural core with Russian, Ukrainian, Gagauz and Soviet influences. It is known for vineyards, enormous underground wine cellars, Orthodox monasteries and fertile rolling countryside. Its capital and largest city is **Chișinău**—pronounced roughly *kish-ih-NOW*. The currency is the **Moldovan leu (MDL)**. [Romanian is the official language](https://inimi.igm.gov.md/en/republic-of-moldova).

### People and language

The 2024 census counted about **2.4 million usual residents**, excluding most territory controlled by Transnistria; Moldova has experienced substantial population decline because of emigration, low birth rates and aging.

Romanian is the state language, although many residents traditionally call their language “Moldovan.” Linguistically, these refer to essentially the same language, but the terminology carries political and identity significance. Russian is widely understood, particularly in cities and minority communities, while Gagauz, Ukrainian and Bulgarian are also spoken. Most residents identify as Orthodox Christian. [The 2024 census recorded 77.2% as ethnically Moldovan and 7.9% as Romanian](https://statistica.gov.md/en/preliminary-results-of-the-2024-population-%E6%BE%B3%E9%97%A8%E8%B5%8C%E5%9C%BA%E5%9C%A8%E7%BA%BF-housing-census-10077_61626.html).

### A very short history

- Most of present-day Moldova belonged to the medieval **Principality of Moldavia**, which also included territory now in Romania.
- The eastern portion, generally called **Bessarabia**, entered the Russian Empire in 1812.
- Bessarabia became part of Romania in 1918.
- The Soviet Union annexed it in 1940 and created the Moldavian Soviet Socialist Republic, combining most of Bessarabia with territory east of the Dniester River.
- Moldova declared independence from the USSR on **27 August 1991**.
- A short war in 1992 left **Transnistria** outside the effective control of Moldova’s central government. [CRS provides a useful historical overview](https://www.everycrsreport.com/reports/R48664.html).

This history explains why questions of Romanian versus Moldovan identity, relations with Russia and orientation toward Europe remain sensitive.

### Government and present direction

Moldova is a **parliamentary republic** with a directly elected president. As of **24 October 2026**:

- **President:** [Maia Sandu](https://presedinte.md/eng/biography), serving her second term.
- **Prime minister:** [Vasile Tofan](https://www.gov.md/index.php/ro/comunicate-de-presa/guvernul-condus-de-prim-ministrul-vasile-tofan-depus-juramantul-de-investire), whose government took office in July 2026.

The constitution declares Moldova permanently neutral, so it is not a NATO member. Its current strategic priority is European integration. Moldova became an **EU candidate in 2022**, formally opened accession negotiations in June 2024 and, most recently, opened additional negotiation clusters concerning the internal market, competitiveness and inclusive growth on 13 October 2026. It is **not yet an EU or Schengen member**. [EU Council accession timeline](https://www.consilium.europa.eu/policies/moldova/).

### Transnistria and Gagauzia

**Transnistria** is a narrow, predominantly Russian-speaking region mainly east of the Dniester—or *Nistru*—River. It has its own de facto administration, currency and security forces, but internationally it is recognized as Moldovan territory. Russian troops remain stationed there, and negotiations have not produced a final settlement.

**Gagauzia**, in southern Moldova, is different: it is a legally recognized autonomous region within Moldova. The Gagauz are a predominantly Orthodox Christian, Turkic-speaking people, although Russian is also commonly used.

### Economy

The World Bank classifies Moldova as an **upper-middle-income economy**. Agriculture and food production remain important—especially grapes, wine, fruit, sunflower products and cereals—alongside manufacturing, trade, technology and other services.

Its main structural problems include:

- extensive labor migration and dependence on remittances;
- an aging and shrinking population;
- rural poverty and weak productivity;
- energy vulnerability;
- economic spillovers from Russia’s war against Ukraine.

EU accession is intended to anchor reforms, improve institutions and integrate Moldova more closely into the European market. [World Bank country overview](https://www.worldbank.org/ext/en/country/moldova).

### Culture, food and wine

Moldovan culture shares much with Romania but also reflects Ukrainian, Russian, Bulgarian, Gagauz, Jewish and Ottoman-era influences. Hospitality, family meals, village traditions and seasonal celebrations are particularly important.

Foods to try include:

- **mămăligă** — cornmeal polenta, often served with cheese, sour cream or meat;
- **plăcinte** — pastries filled with cheese, potato, cabbage, pumpkin or fruit;
- **sarmale** — stuffed cabbage or vine leaves;
- **zeamă** — chicken-and-noodle soup flavored with lovage;
- local fruit, preserves, brandy and wine.  
  [Official Moldovan gastronomy guide](https://moldova.travel/en/gastronomy/).

Wine is central to the country’s identity. **Cricova** has an underground “wine city,” while **Mileștii Mici** is known for an exceptionally large underground bottle collection.

### What travelers usually visit

- **Chișinău:** leafy parks, museums, markets, Soviet-era architecture, cafés and wine bars.
- **Orheiul Vechi:** a dramatic river valley containing archaeological remains, villages and cave monasteries.
- **Cricova and Mileștii Mici:** underground winery tours.
- **Soroca:** a fortress on the Dniester and a notable Roma community.
- **Gagauzia:** especially Comrat, for a different linguistic and culinary culture.
- Rural guesthouses, monasteries and the Lower Prut region.  
  [Official tourism overview](https://moldova.travel/en/places-to-visit/).

Late spring and early autumn generally offer the most comfortable weather; October is particularly attractive for wine-related events.

### Practical and safety notes

Cards and ATMs are common in cities, but cash remains useful in villages. The emergency number is **112**. Entry rules depend on nationality, so travelers should verify them before departure.

As of 24 October 2026, the U.S. travel advisory rates Moldova **Level 2—exercise increased caution**, citing regional-security concerns, unexploded ordnance in some rural or former conflict areas and petty crime. It advises travelers to **reconsider travel to Transnistria**, where consular assistance can be limited, checkpoints are unpredictable and photographing military facilities can lead to detention. [Current advisory](https://travel.state.gov/en/international-travel/travel-advisories/moldova.html).

- an aging and shrinking population;
- rural poverty and weak productivity;
- energy vulnerability;
- economic spillovers from Russia’s war against Ukraine.

- **plăcinte** — pastries filled with cheese, potato, cabbage, pumpkin or fruit;
- **sarmale** — stuffed cabbage or vine leaves;
- **zeamă** — chicken-and-noodle soup flavored with lovage;

- **Orheiul Vechi:** a dramatic river valley containing archaeological remains, villages and cave monasteries.
- **Cricova and Mileștii Mici:** underground winery tours.
- **Soroca:** a fortress on the Dniester and a notable Roma community.
- **Gagauzia:** especially Comrat, for a different linguistic and culinary culture.

### Practical and safety notes

As of 24 October 2026, the U.S. travel advisory rates Moldova **Level 2—exercise increased caution**, citing regional-security concerns, unexploded ordnance in some rural or former conflict areas and petty crime. It advises travelers to **reconsider travel to Transnistria**, where consular assistance can be limited, checkpoints are unpredictable and photographing military facilities can lead to detention. Indonesia has many volcanoes and earthquakes because it sits where several moving tectonic plates meet—part of the **Pacific “Ring of Fire.”** The most important are the Indo-Australian, Sunda/Eurasian, Pacific, and Philippine Sea plates, together with numerous smaller crustal blocks. [Indonesia’s BMKG](https://pgt.bmkg.go.id/detail/artikel/6) identifies these interacting plates as the main cause of the country’s seismic activity.

### How this produces earthquakes

Along Sumatra, Java, Bali, and Nusa Tenggara, the dense oceanic part of the Indo-Australian Plate is being forced beneath the Sunda Plate. This process, called **subduction**, occurs along the Sunda–Java Trench.

The plates do not slide smoothly. Their boundary can lock while motion continues, accumulating stress. When the fault suddenly slips, it releases energy as an earthquake. Indonesia consequently experiences:

- **Megathrust earthquakes** on the boundary between the plates;
- **Deeper earthquakes** inside the descending plate;
- **Shallow earthquakes** on faults within the overriding plate, such as the Great Sumatran Fault;
- Additional earthquakes from the especially complicated collisions and faults around Sulawesi, Maluku, and Papua.

Subduction zones can produce Earth’s most powerful earthquakes. If an offshore earthquake abruptly displaces the seabed, it can also generate a tsunami. [The USGS explains these subduction-zone processes](https://www.usgs.gov/special-topics/subduction-zone-science/science/introduction-subduction-zones-amazing-events).

### How this produces volcanoes

As the descending oceanic plate sinks, it carries water in minerals and sediments into the mantle. That water lowers the melting temperature of the surrounding mantle, generating magma. Because magma is buoyant, it rises through the crust and sometimes erupts.

This creates long chains of volcanoes—**volcanic arcs**—roughly parallel to the offshore trenches. Indonesia contains several, including the Sunda, Banda, Sangihe, and Halmahera arcs. The Smithsonian’s Global Volcanism Program lists **101 Indonesian volcanoes with evidence of activity during the Holocene**, though “Holocene volcano” does not necessarily mean presently erupting. [Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program](https://volcano.si.edu/volcanolist_countries.cfm?country=Indonesia).

In short, **both hazards have the same underlying cause: Indonesia lies above multiple active plate boundaries, especially subduction zones**. Earthquakes result mainly from sudden movement along those boundaries and related faults; volcanoes form because subduction helps generate magma. Most Indonesian earthquakes are tectonic, not caused by volcanoes.

## Japan in brief

Japan is an island country in East Asia known for combining deep historical traditions with advanced industry and distinctive contemporary culture. Its landscape ranges from snowy Hokkaido to subtropical Okinawa, while its cities range from temple-rich Kyoto to metropolitan Tokyo.

### Key facts—as of October 24, 2026

- **Capital:** Tokyo  
- **Population:** approximately **122.69 million**, based on the provisional October 1, 2026 estimate; the population is declining. [Statistics Bureau of Japan](https://www.stat.go.jp/data/jinsui/)
- **Area:** about **377,975 km²**
- **Administrative divisions:** 47 prefectures
- **Currency:** Japanese yen, **JPY/¥**
- **Main language:** Japanese, written with kanji, hiragana, and katakana
- **Government:** Parliamentary constitutional monarchy with a bicameral legislature called the National Diet
- **Emperor:** Naruhito, whose constitutional role is symbolic; he acceded in 2019. [Imperial Household Agency](https://www.kunaicho.go.jp/en/learn/about/history/history01.html)
- **Prime minister:** **Sanae Takaichi** as of the date above. [Prime Minister’s Office](https://japan.kantei.go.jp/105/speech/202610/15kaiken.html)

The Diet consists of a 465-member House of Representatives and a 248-member House of Councillors. Under Japan’s postwar constitution, sovereignty belongs to the people and the emperor is “the symbol of the State and of the unity of the people.” [Government of Japan](https://www.japan.go.jp/japan/index.html)

## Geography and climate

Japan’s four largest islands are:

1. **Honshu** — Tokyo, Kyoto, Osaka, Hiroshima and Mount Fuji  
2. **Hokkaido** — colder, spacious and famous for snow  
3. **Kyushu** — volcanoes, hot springs and cities such as Fukuoka and Nagasaki  
4. **Shikoku** — mountains, small cities and an important Buddhist pilgrimage route  

The Okinawa and Ryukyu island chains extend southwest toward Taiwan and have their own historical and cultural identity.

Much of Japan is mountainous and forested, so most people live on comparatively narrow coastal plains. Its position along the Pacific “Ring of Fire” makes earthquakes, volcanoes and tsunamis important realities. Summers are generally hot and humid; northern and Sea of Japan regions can receive heavy winter snow. The rainy season usually begins around May or June, while typhoons are a particular concern in late summer and early autumn. [Japan National Tourism Organization](https://www.japan.travel/en/plan/weather/)

## A short historical outline

- **Ancient Japan:** Early societies included the Jōmon culture. Rice agriculture and metallurgy later arrived from the Asian continent. Buddhism reached Japan through Korea and China in the sixth century.
- **Courtly period:** Nara became a permanent capital in 710, followed by Kyoto in 794. The Heian court produced works such as *The Tale of Genji*.
- **Samurai rule:** From the late 12th century, military governments known as shogunates held effective power. Samurai and regional lords dominated politics.
- **Tokugawa era, 1603–1867:** Japan experienced more than two centuries of relative peace, controlled foreign contact and growing urban culture. Kabuki, ukiyo-e prints and early forms of modern sushi flourished.
- **Meiji transformation:** Beginning in 1868, Japan rapidly industrialized and built a modern centralized state.
- **Empire and war:** Imperial Japan expanded across Asia through colonialism and war. Its conflict with China and later the Allied powers ended with defeat in 1945 after the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki.
- **Postwar Japan:** A democratic, pacifist constitution took effect in 1947. Rapid economic growth made Japan an industrial and technological power; the 1964 Tokyo Olympics and the first shinkansen symbolized its recovery. [JNTO history overview](https://www.japan.travel/en/responsible-travel-guide/features/overview-japanese-history/)

## Culture and society

Japanese culture is not uniform: Hokkaido, Okinawa, Kansai, Tōhoku and other regions possess distinctive dialects, foods and historical experiences.

**Religion** is often practiced flexibly. Shinto shrines and Buddhist temples coexist, and many people participate in customs associated with both without necessarily describing themselves as strongly religious.

Traditional arts include tea ceremony, calligraphy, ceramics, flower arrangement, gardens, Noh and Kabuki theater, woodblock printing and martial arts. Modern Japan has been equally influential through architecture, fashion, cinema, manga, anime, video games and popular music.

Japanese food is highly regional. Besides sushi, widely encountered foods include ramen, soba and udon noodles, tempura, yakitori, curry rice, okonomiyaki, tonkatsu and seasonal multi-course *kaiseki*. Convenience stores and department-store food halls are also significant parts of everyday food culture.

UNESCO lists **27 Japanese World Heritage properties** as of 2026—22 cultural and five natural—including Kyoto’s monuments, Himeji Castle, the Hiroshima Peace Memorial, Mount Fuji, Yakushima and Shiretoko. [UNESCO](https://whc.unesco.org/en/statesparties/JP/)

## Economy and present-day challenges

Japan remains one of the world’s largest economies. World Bank data put its 2025 nominal GDP at approximately **US$4.44 trillion**. It is particularly important in automobiles, industrial machinery, electronics, robotics, advanced materials and precision manufacturing. [World Bank](https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/NY.GDP.MKTP.CD?locations=JP)

Major challenges include:

- A rapidly aging and shrinking population
- Labor shortages
- Concentration of people and opportunities in large metropolitan areas
- High public debt
- Energy security and decarbonization
- Managing earthquake, tsunami and climate-related risks

The IMF reported in 2026 that domestic demand and employment remained relatively resilient, but identified aging, public debt and cost-of-living pressures as major long-term issues. [International Monetary Fund](https://www.imf.org/en/publications/cr/issues/2026/04/02/japan-2026-article-iv-consultation-press-release-staff-report-and-statement-by-the-executive-director-for-japan)

## For a first-time traveler

A classic first trip combines:

- **Tokyo:** museums, neighborhoods, food and contemporary culture
- **Kyoto:** temples, gardens and traditional districts
- **Osaka:** street food and lively urban culture
- **Nara:** early Buddhist monuments and historic parkland
- **Hiroshima and Miyajima:** modern history and Itsukushima Shrine

With more time, consider Hokkaido, Kanazawa and the Japanese Alps, the Seto Inland Sea, Kyushu’s hot-spring towns, or Okinawa.

Spring and autumn usually offer comfortable weather but can be crowded. Golden Week, Obon and New Year are especially busy. Public transportation is generally efficient; on some shinkansen services, very large luggage requires advance arrangements. Carrying some cash remains advisable outside major centers.

Basic etiquette emphasizes consideration for others: queue properly, speak quietly on trains, remove shoes where indicated, arrive punctually and wash before entering a communal hot-spring bath. [JNTO etiquette guide](https://www.japan.travel/en/responsible-travel-guide/japanese-customs-and-etiquette/)

Entry and visa requirements depend on nationality and can change, so travelers should consult Japan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs before departure.

- **Samurai rule:** From the late 12th century, military governments known as shogunates held effective power. Samurai and regional lords dominated politics.
- **Tokugawa era, 1603–1867:** Japan experienced more than two centuries of relative peace, controlled foreign contact and growing urban culture. Kabuki, ukiyo-e prints and early forms of modern sushi flourished.
- **Meiji transformation:** Beginning in 1868, Japan rapidly industrialized and built a modern centralized state.
- **Empire and war:** Imperial Japan expanded across Asia through colonialism and war. Its conflict with China and later the Allied powers ended with defeat in 1945 after the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

- A rapidly aging and shrinking population
- Labor shortages
- Concentration of people and opportunities in large metropolitan areas
- High public debt
- Energy security and decarbonization
- Managing earthquake, tsunami and climate-related risks

- **Tokyo:** museums, neighborhoods, food and contemporary culture
- **Kyoto:** temples, gardens and traditional districts
- **Osaka:** street food and lively urban culture
- **Nara:** early Buddhist monuments and historic parkland
- **Hiroshima and Miyajima:** modern history and Itsukushima Shrine

Spring and autumn usually offer comfortable weather but can be crowded. Golden Week, Obon and New Year are especially busy. Public transportation is generally efficient; on some shinkansen services, very large luggage requires advance arrangements. Carrying some cash remains advisable outside major centers.

Entry and visa requirements depend on nationality and can change, so travelers should consult Japan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs before departure.

## Overview

Both Ethiopia and Kenya lie in eastern Africa and are crossed by the East African Rift system, but their landscapes differ markedly: **Ethiopia is a larger, landlocked country dominated by rugged highlands**, whereas **Kenya straddles the Equator, has an Indian Ocean coast, and contains broader plains and savannas alongside its central highlands**.

| Feature | Ethiopia | Kenya |
|---|---|---|
| **Location** | Horn of Africa, immediately north of Kenya; landlocked | Equatorial East Africa, with an Indian Ocean coastline |
| **Size** | About 1.1 million km²—nearly twice Kenya’s area | About 580,000 km² |
| **Dominant terrain** | Extensive mountains, deeply dissected plateaus and peripheral lowlands | Coastal plain, interior plateaus, central highlands, Rift Valley and broad savannas |
| **Rift Valley** | Runs mainly southwest–northeast, separating western and southeastern highlands | Runs broadly north–south through the central highlands |
| **Highest terrain** | Ras Dashen, approximately 4,550 m | Mount Kenya, 5,199 m; Kenya has the higher individual summit |
| **Major waters** | Lake Tana and the headwaters of the Blue Nile; Awash, Omo and numerous Rift Valley lakes | Lake Victoria’s eastern shore, most of Lake Turkana, Rift lakes, and the Tana River |
| **Main climate pattern** | Cool-to-temperate highlands surrounded by hot, often arid lowlands | Hot, humid coast; mild highlands; extensive arid and semi-arid north and east |

### Geography

**Ethiopia’s defining feature is its highland mass.** Much of the country consists of elevated volcanic plateaus cut by steep river gorges. The surrounding lowlands include the extremely hot Afar Depression in the northeast and dry plains toward Somalia in the east and southeast. Rivers flow outward from the highlands: westward toward the Nile system, southeastward toward Somalia, or internally through the Rift Valley. Lake Tana is the source of the Blue Nile. [British Geological Survey](https://earthwise.bgs.ac.uk/index.php/Hydrogeology_of_Ethiopia)

**Kenya has a more gradual east-to-west sequence of landscapes.** A low, humid coastal plain rises through dry bushland and plateaus to the fertile central highlands. The Rift Valley divides these highlands and contains escarpments, volcanoes and lakes. Farther west, the land descends toward Lake Victoria, while most of northern and eastern Kenya consists of sparsely watered plains. [Kenya Embassy](https://kenyaembassydc.org/aboutkenyageography/)

Thus, Ethiopia is generally **more rugged and elevated as a whole**, while Kenya has **greater access to marine environments and more extensive lowland savannas**. The countries are also hydrologically connected: Ethiopia’s Omo River supplies most of the water entering Kenya’s Lake Turkana.

### Climate

Neither country has one uniform climate; in both, **elevation is often more important than latitude**.

#### Ethiopia

- The central and northern highlands are relatively mild or cool despite their tropical latitude.
- The Afar, Somali and other lowlands are much hotter and drier.
- The southwest is generally the wettest part of the country, while the northeast and southeast can be desert-like.
- Across much of the central, northern and western country, the principal rainy season—**Kiremt**—runs approximately from mid-June to mid-September.
- A smaller and less reliable **Belg** rainy period occurs roughly from February to May.
- Southern and southeastern districts often have a more distinctly **bimodal** rainfall pattern.
- Rainfall is highly variable from year to year, making drought a recurrent hazard; heavy seasonal rain can also cause flooding and erosion. [World Bank Climate Risk Profile](https://climateknowledgeportal.worldbank.org/sites/default/files/2021-05/15463A-WB_Ethiopia%20Country%20Profile-WEB.pdf)

#### Kenya

- The Indian Ocean coast is **tropical, hot and humid**, with a stronger maritime and monsoonal influence than anywhere in Ethiopia.
- The central highlands—including Nairobi—are considerably milder because of elevation.
- Northern and eastern Kenya are predominantly **arid or semi-arid**.
- Much of the country has two rainy seasons: the **long rains** from about March to May and the **short rains** from October to December.
- Western Kenya and the Lake Victoria basin are generally wetter and may receive rain outside those periods because of lake and regional atmospheric influences.
- June through August is usually the coolest period, while February and March are commonly among the hottest months.
- Kenya is also highly exposed to recurrent droughts, irregular rainy seasons and episodic flooding. [Red Cross Red Crescent Climate Centre](https://www.climatecentre.org/wp-content/uploads/RCCC-Country-profiles-Kenya_2022-V2-Final.pdf)

### Bottom line

- **Ethiopia:** larger, landlocked, more continuously mountainous and dominated by a high plateau; its main northern and central rains occur during the Northern Hemisphere summer.
- **Kenya:** smaller, equatorial and coastal, with a stronger contrast between humid coast, temperate highlands and expansive dry plains; much of it has spring and autumn rainy seasons.
- **Both:** have dramatic elevation-driven climate zones, fertile highlands, Rift Valley landscapes, hot dry lowlands and substantial vulnerability to drought and floods.

Bolivia is often said to have **two capitals**, but legally the distinction is:

- **Sucre is the constitutional and official capital.**
- **La Paz is the seat of government—the de facto administrative capital.**

| City | Main role |
|---|---|
| **Sucre** | Named the capital by Article 6 of Bolivia’s Constitution. It is the center of the **judicial branch**, including the Supreme Tribunal of Justice and other high courts. |
| **La Paz** | Houses the **president and executive ministries**, the **Plurinational Legislative Assembly**, and the national electoral authority. Most embassies are also based there. |

### Why the split happened

Sucre became the official capital in 1839. By the late nineteenth century, however, political and economic influence was shifting north toward La Paz as the southern silver economy declined and the tin economy grew.

In 1898, politicians based in Sucre passed a law requiring the president to remain there. This intensified the struggle between Sucre-based Conservatives and La Paz-based Liberals, helping trigger the **Federal War of 1898–99**. The Liberals won, and La Paz became the **de facto seat of government** in 1899. But Sucre was never formally stripped of its status as capital, and the highest judicial institutions remained there. [Bolivia’s official historical account](https://www.ine.gob.bo/index.php/bolivia/aspectos-historicos/) describes this transition.

So, in everyday terms: **La Paz runs the national government, while Sucre retains the legal title of capital and anchors the judiciary.** The Library of Congress summarizes the arrangement as “La Paz—executive and legislative; Sucre—constitutional and judicial.” [Library of Congress](https://guides.loc.gov/bolivia-country-guide)

**Climate, pastoralism and borders shape Sahelian life through one central fact: people must remain mobile in a highly variable environment, while states increasingly try to regulate that mobility.** Pastoralism is therefore not simply a response to poverty; it is a sophisticated way of using scattered water and pasture. Borders can either support this adaptation—through open routes, markets and veterinary cooperation—or turn climatic stress into economic hardship and conflict.

### 1. Climate sets the rhythm of life

The Sahel is a broad transition zone between the Sahara and the wetter savannas to the south. In much of West Africa it receives roughly **150–600 mm of rain annually**, concentrated in a short wet season, followed by an eight- or nine-month dry season. Rainfall varies sharply from year to year and even between nearby places. These are ecological gradients, not fixed lines on a map. [U.S. Geological Survey](https://www.usgs.gov/centers/eros/science/bioclimatic-regions-map)

That variability determines:

- when farmers plant millet, sorghum and groundnuts;
- where wells, ponds and grazing areas remain usable;
- when herds move north or south;
- livestock health and market prices;
- the timing of the annual “lean season,” when food stocks are low;
- whether household members seek seasonal work in towns or abroad.

Climate change does **not** mean that every part of the Sahel is simply becoming steadily drier. After the severe droughts of the 1970s and 1980s, parts of the region experienced a partial rainfall recovery. But temperatures are rising, evaporation is increasing, and rainfall is becoming more erratic: intense downpours and floods can occur alongside longer dry spells. The IPCC reports increasing drought risk, heavier rainfall events and major uncertainty over where future rainfall will rise or fall across the western and eastern Sahel. [IPCC](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg2/chapter/chapter-9/)

Thus, **timing and reliability often matter more than the annual rainfall total**. A heavy storm may produce an impressive total but destroy crops or run off hardened soil without replenishing pasture and groundwater.

### 2. Pastoralism turns variability into a livelihood

Pastoralism works by moving animals—cattle, sheep, goats and camels—to where vegetation and water are temporarily available. **Transhumance** means regular seasonal movement, often between established wet- and dry-season grazing areas; it is not aimless wandering.

A common pattern is to move south during the dry season toward water, crop residues and markets, then return north after the rains, when fresh grass becomes available and southern fields are planted. Routes can extend hundreds of kilometres and cross several countries. The exact pattern differs greatly by location and community.

Mobility provides several advantages:

- animals convert plants unsuitable for human consumption into milk, meat, hides, transport and savings;
- moving herds avoids exhausting a single pasture;
- livestock serve as assets that can be sold after a poor harvest;
- manure fertilizes fields, while herds consume post-harvest crop residues;
- northern livestock economies supply rapidly growing southern and coastal cities.

Consequently, farmers and herders are not always separate groups. Many households are **agropastoral**, combining crops, livestock, trading, remittances and seasonal employment. FAO describes pastoralism as a major economic and cultural system extending across West and Central Africa, with routes linking Sahelian and coastal countries. [FAO Pastoralist Knowledge Hub](https://www.fao.org/pastoralist-knowledge-hub/pastoralist-networks/regional-networks/west-and-central-africa/en)

Mobility also creates difficulties. Mobile families can be missed by censuses and social-protection systems, while children may have trouble attending conventional schools and families may be far from clinics, veterinary services and formal markets. Women and poorer herd owners are especially vulnerable when livestock losses reduce access to milk, income or property.

### 3. Borders cut across ecological and social regions

Modern borders divide grazing systems, markets, ethnic communities and river basins that long predate the states themselves. For a pastoral household, an international border may run through what is functionally one economic landscape: pasture on one side, a livestock market on another, relatives elsewhere and a veterinary post in a fourth place.

Borders can be helpful when governments cooperate. They provide places for:

- animal-health inspections and vaccination;
- recognized transhumance corridors;
- market regulation;
- mediation between visiting herders and host communities;
- disease surveillance and drought early-warning systems.

ECOWAS adopted a regional decision regulating transhumance in 1998, and international transhumance certificates have been used to facilitate authorized cross-border movement. [ECOWAS decision](https://ecowap.ecowas.int/see-document/21) Regional projects have also built water points, marked corridors, vaccinated livestock and improved livestock markets. [World Bank](https://www.worldbank.org/en/results/2020/10/19/improving-productivity-for-pastoralists-and-agro-pastoralists-across-the-sahel)

But borders also create obstacles:

- permits, checkpoints, informal payments and confiscation;
- sudden closures during epidemics, political disputes or military operations;
- different land, veterinary and grazing rules in neighbouring states;
- restrictions imposed because pastoral movement is associated—often unfairly—with smuggling or insurgency;
- concentration of stranded animals near border wells and farms.

The regional legal landscape has also become less certain. Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger formally left ECOWAS on 29 January 2025. ECOWAS’s published transitional arrangement nevertheless asked states to preserve visa-free movement and existing treatment of goods from those countries “until further notice.” [ECOWAS](https://www.ecowas.int/press-statement-2/) Such political changes matter because pastoral livelihoods depend on predictable rules extending beyond any one state.

### 4. The interaction can produce cooperation—or conflict

Imagine that rains begin late. Herders leave northern pastures earlier than expected and arrive in a farming district before crops have been harvested. If an established corridor has been cultivated, a border is closed or a water point has been privatized, animals may enter fields or crowd around the remaining wells. A dispute over crop damage can then acquire ethnic or political meaning.

But climate does **not directly or inevitably cause war or terrorism**. Whether scarcity becomes violence depends on land rights, policing, access to weapons, political exclusion, corruption, local mediation and the behaviour of armed groups. Recent research in the central Sahel found indirect pathways—through disrupted production, competition and weakened conflict management—rather than a simple climate-to-terrorism link. [Institute for Security Studies](https://issafrica.org/iss-today/does-climate-change-fuel-terrorism-in-the-sahel)

Insecurity also works in the opposite direction: armed violence closes markets and roads, prevents veterinary campaigns, displaces farmers and herders, and makes traditional negotiations dangerous. Climate stress, weak governance and conflict therefore reinforce one another.

### What improves resilience?

The most effective policies generally **manage mobility rather than trying to eliminate it**:

1. Legally protect grazing land, corridors and access to water.
2. Coordinate transhumance dates and border procedures between states.
3. Include pastoral representatives, farmers and traditional authorities in local agreements.
4. Expand weather information, livestock vaccination and drought early warning.
5. Provide mobile schools, clinics, veterinary teams and portable social benefits.
6. Keep livestock markets and trade routes open where security permits.
7. Recognize women’s and young people’s economic roles and land rights.
8. Avoid creating permanent water points without plans for grazing pressure and conflict management.

The African Union similarly treats secure pastoral mobility and inclusive resource governance as central to both adaptation and conflict prevention. [African Union](https://au.int/en/documents/20221129/guidelines-secure-pastoralism-and-prevent-conflicts-africa-secure-peaceful-and)

**In short:** climate makes resources seasonal and unpredictable; pastoralism uses movement to cope with that uncertainty; and borders determine whether movement remains a source of resilience and trade or becomes costly, dangerous and conflict-prone.

Lesotho is independent because **it was never part of the modern South African state**. Its enclosure is a result of colonial borders, not a sign that it separated from South Africa.

- In the early 1800s, **King Moshoeshoe I united the Basotho** into a distinct kingdom. After losing considerable land in wars with Boer settlers from the Orange Free State, he requested British protection. Britain declared Basutoland a protectorate in **1868**, preserving the mountainous territorial core that became Lesotho. [South African History Online](https://sahistory.org.za/dated-event/basutoland-now-lesotho-becomes-british-territory)
- Britain annexed Basutoland to the Cape Colony in 1871, but Basotho resistance—especially during the **Gun War of 1880–81**—made Cape rule unsuccessful. In 1884 Britain removed Basutoland from Cape administration and restored direct imperial rule. [Oxford Research Encyclopedia of African History](https://academic.oup.com/edited-volume/61663/chapter-abstract/553404460)
- When the **Union of South Africa** was created in 1910, it combined the Cape, Natal, Transvaal and Orange Free State—but excluded Basutoland, Bechuanaland and Swaziland. Britain worried about placing their African populations under South Africa’s white-minority government, although eventual incorporation was initially contemplated. [South African History Online](https://sahistory.org.za/article/constructing-union-south-africa-negotiations-contestations-1902-10)
- South Africa subsequently sought control of Basutoland, but Basotho political opposition remained strong. Incorporation became even less acceptable after South Africa’s National Party introduced apartheid in 1948. British records describe the proposed transfer as increasingly untenable during this period. [The National Archives](https://cdn.nationalarchives.gov.uk/documents/migrated-archives-guidance.pdf)
- Britain instead granted Basutoland independence as the **Kingdom of Lesotho on 4 October 1966**. [UK Lesotho Independence Act 1966](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1966/24/data.htm?timeline=false)

So the simplest explanation is: **the Basotho kingdom survived conquest by accepting British protection; Britain kept it administratively separate when South Africa was formed; and it later decolonized as its own country.** The surrounding territories became South Africa, leaving Lesotho as an enclave.

As of **October 24, 2026**, the principal **standardized quantum-resistant digital-signature algorithms** are:

| Algorithm | Type | Status | Best suited for |
|---|---|---|---|
| **ML-DSA** | Module-lattice based | **NIST FIPS 204, final** | General-purpose signing; usually the default choice |
| **SLH-DSA** | Stateless hash based | **NIST FIPS 205, final** | A conservative, non-lattice alternative where larger signatures are acceptable |
| **LMS/HSS** | Stateful hash based | **NIST SP 800-208; RFC 8554** | Firmware, secure boot and tightly controlled signing systems |
| **XMSS/XMSS-MT** | Stateful hash based | **NIST SP 800-208; RFC 8391** | Similar specialized, long-lived signing applications |
| **FN-DSA** | NTRU-lattice based | Selected by NIST; **FIPS 206 not yet final** | Potentially useful when small signatures and fast verification matter, but not yet the normal standards-based deployment choice |

### 1. ML-DSA — recommended general-purpose choice

**ML-DSA**, derived from **CRYSTALS-Dilithium**, is standardized in FIPS 204. It provides three parameter sets:

- `ML-DSA-44`
- `ML-DSA-65`
- `ML-DSA-87`

It offers a practical balance of performance, key size, signature size and implementation simplicity. For new general-purpose systems, this is normally the first algorithm to evaluate. Use the finalized **ML-DSA specification**, rather than assuming an older “Dilithium” implementation is automatically wire-compatible with FIPS 204. [NIST FIPS 204](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/204/final)

### 2. SLH-DSA — conservative hash-based alternative

**SLH-DSA**, based on **SPHINCS+**, is standardized in FIPS 205. Its security relies principally on well-studied hash-function properties rather than lattice problems.

Advantages:

- Stateless: the signer does not have to remember which one-time key state was used.
- Provides cryptographic diversity from lattice-based ML-DSA.
- Often attractive as a fallback if a new lattice weakness were discovered.

Disadvantages:

- Signatures are much larger.
- Signing and verification are generally slower than ML-DSA.

It has SHA-2 and SHAKE variants at approximately 128-, 192- and 256-bit security levels, with “fast” and “small-signature” parameter choices. [NIST FIPS 205](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/205/final)

### 3. LMS/HSS and XMSS/XMSS-MT — quantum-resistant but stateful

These Merkle-tree/hash-based schemes are also considered quantum resistant:

- **LMS**, generally deployed hierarchically as **HSS**
- **XMSS**, including the multi-tree **XMSS-MT**

Their critical limitation is **state management**. Each signing state must be used only as specified; restoring an old backup, cloning a signer or allowing two devices to use the same state can enable forgery. Consequently, they are not convenient replacements for RSA or ECDSA in ordinary applications. They are most appropriate for controlled use cases such as firmware signing and secure boot. [NIST SP 800-208](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/208/final), [IETF RFC 9958](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9958.html)

### 4. FN-DSA/FALCON — selected, but wait for the final standard

**FN-DSA**, derived from **FALCON**, is another lattice-based quantum-resistant signature scheme. It offers small keys and signatures and fast verification, but safe implementation—particularly signing, floating-point arithmetic and side-channel protection—is comparatively difficult.

NIST selected it for FIPS 206, but it was not yet a finalized NIST standard as of the stated date. Unless a particular profile explicitly requires it, ML-DSA or SLH-DSA is the safer standards-based deployment choice. [NIST PQC signature project](https://csrc.nist.gov/Projects/pqc-dig-sig)

## Algorithms that are **not** quantum resistant

A sufficiently capable quantum computer running Shor’s algorithm would break signature systems based on integer factorization or discrete logarithms, including:

- **RSA signatures**, including RSA-PSS
- **DSA**
- **ECDSA**
- **Ed25519 and Ed448**
- **Schnorr signatures** over conventional elliptic curves
- Pairing-based signatures such as **BLS** and **BBS**

Using larger RSA or elliptic-curve keys does not fix the fundamental quantum vulnerability.

## Practical recommendation

- **New general-purpose system:** use **ML-DSA**.
- **Need a structurally different fallback:** consider **SLH-DSA**.
- **Firmware or secure boot with rigorously controlled hardware state:** LMS/HSS or XMSS may be suitable.
- **Migration requiring compatibility with classical systems:** use a protocol-defined **hybrid signature** combining, for example, ML-DSA with ECDSA or RSA—but do not invent an ad-hoc combiner.
- Prefer vetted cryptographic libraries and finalized protocol profiles; “post-quantum” means *believed resistant under current cryptanalysis*, not mathematically guaranteed to remain secure forever.

- Stateless: the signer does not have to remember which one-time key state was used.
- Provides cryptographic diversity from lattice-based ML-DSA.
- Often attractive as a fallback if a new lattice weakness were discovered.

Disadvantages:

- Signatures are much larger.
- Signing and verification are generally slower than ML-DSA.

It has SHA-2 and SHAKE variants at approximately 128-, 192- and 256-bit security levels, with “fast” and “small-signature” parameter choices. [NIST FIPS 205](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/205/final)

### 3. LMS/HSS and XMSS/XMSS-MT — quantum-resistant but stateful

These Merkle-tree/hash-based schemes are also considered quantum resistant:

- **LMS**, generally deployed hierarchically as **HSS**
- **XMSS**, including the multi-tree **XMSS-MT**

Their critical limitation is **state management**. Each signing state must be used only as specified; restoring an old backup, cloning a signer or allowing two devices to use the same state can enable forgery. Consequently, they are not convenient replacements for RSA or ECDSA in ordinary applications. They are most appropriate for controlled use cases such as firmware signing and secure boot. [NIST SP 800-208](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/208/final), [IETF RFC 9958](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9958.html)

### 4. FN-DSA/FALCON — selected, but wait for the final standard

**FN-DSA**, derived from **FALCON**, is another lattice-based quantum-resistant signature scheme. It offers small keys and signatures and fast verification, but safe implementation—particularly signing, floating-point arithmetic and side-channel protection—is comparatively difficult.

NIST selected it for FIPS 206, but it was not yet a finalized NIST standard as of the stated date. Unless a particular profile explicitly requires it, ML-DSA or SLH-DSA is the safer standards-based deployment choice. [NIST PQC signature project](https://csrc.nist.gov/Projects/pqc-dig-sig)

## Algorithms that are **not** quantum resistant

A sufficiently capable quantum computer running Shor’s algorithm would break signature systems based on integer factorization or discrete logarithms, including:

- **RSA signatures**, including RSA-PSS
- **DSA**
- **ECDSA**
- **Ed25519 and Ed448**
- **Schnorr signatures** over conventional elliptic curves
- Pairing-based signatures such as **BLS** and **BBS**

Using larger RSA or elliptic-curve keys does not fix the fundamental quantum vulnerability.

## Practical recommendation

- **New general-purpose system:** use **ML-DSA**.
- **Need a structurally different fallback:** consider **SLH-DSA**.
- **Firmware or secure boot with rigorously controlled hardware state:** LMS/HSS or XMSS may be suitable.
- **Migration requiring compatibility with classical systems:** use a protocol-defined **hybrid signature** combining, for example, ML-DSA with ECDSA or RSA—but do not invent an ad-hoc combiner.
- Prefer vetted cryptographic libraries and finalized protocol profiles; “post-quantum” means *believed resistant under current cryptanalysis*, not mathematically guaranteed to remain secure forever.

answer:
**Data availability sampling (DAS)** lets Ethereum nodes check that rollup data really exists without every node downloading every byte. It is a probabilistic availability check—not a way to execute the data or prove that every transaction inside it is valid.

## Why Ethereum needs it

Layer-2 rollups execute transactions outside Ethereum, then publish compressed transaction data to Ethereum in temporary **blobs**. That data must be available so that:

- optimistic-rollup verifiers can detect and challenge invalid state transitions;
- ZK-rollup users can reconstruct the rollup’s state and transact independently;
- rollups do not have to trust a sequencer to reveal data later.

Before DAS, every Ethereum consensus node downloaded every blob. Increasing blob capacity would therefore increase every node’s bandwidth and storage requirements, eventually favoring data centers over home nodes.

DAS replaces “everyone downloads everything” with:

> **Each node downloads a small, different portion; collectively, the network covers the whole dataset.**

## How PeerDAS works

Ethereum’s deployed form of DAS is **PeerDAS**, introduced by EIP-7594.

### 1. Erasure-code each blob

A blob contains 4,096 field elements—about 128 KiB. Ethereum interprets those elements as evaluations of a polynomial and uses Reed–Solomon-style erasure coding to extend the blob to twice its original size.

This redundancy means that the original blob can be reconstructed from any sufficiently large half of the extended blob. Consequently, an attacker cannot make even a small, strategically important part unrecoverable without withholding roughly half of the extended data.

### 2. Divide the extended data into cells and columns

Each extended blob is divided into 128 cells. For a block containing several blobs:

- each blob is a **row**;
- cells with the same position across all blobs form a **column**.

PeerDAS distributes these 128 columns over 128 gossip subnets. A sample is therefore a column containing one cell from every blob in that block—not an entire blob.

### 3. Assign different columns to different nodes

A node’s identity deterministically maps it to a pseudorandom subset of column subnets. It must download, retain, and serve those columns during the blob-retention period.

Under the current specification:

- an ordinary non-validating node custodies at least **4 of 128 columns**;
- every node samples at least **8 columns per slot**;
- nodes with validators attached custody at least 8, with the requirement increasing according to their attached validator balance;
- a validator node representing at least 4,096 ETH becomes a **supernode** and custodies all columns.

Although an ordinary node custodies only 4/128 of the *extended* data, the extension doubled the data size, so this equals about **1/8 of the original blob volume**.

### 4. Authenticate every sample with KZG proofs

The block contains a **KZG commitment** for each blob. Every sampled cell comes with a KZG proof showing that it really is the cell at that position in the polynomial committed to by the block.

This separates two questions:

- **Integrity:** Is this cell genuine and consistent with the block’s commitment?  
  KZG proofs answer this.
- **Availability:** Can the network actually supply the cells?  
  Sampling answers this.

A malicious peer cannot satisfy a request by inventing plausible-looking data because the proof would fail.

### 5. Decide whether the data is available

For each slot, a node requests its required columns from peers that advertise custody of them. Sampling succeeds only if the node receives and verifies every selected column.

Validators incorporate that result into fork choice: an honest validator should not vote for a block whose required blob samples cannot be obtained and verified.

## Why a few samples are meaningful

Consider a simplified model. If an unrecoverable dataset requires at least half of the extended pieces to be missing, and a node takes \(s\) independent uniform samples, the probability that every sample accidentally lands in the available half is at most:

\[
\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^s
\]

With eight samples, that simplified per-node probability is at most \(1/256\). But PeerDAS does not rely on one node’s eight samples alone. Thousands of nodes have different pseudorandom assignments, custody data, query multiple peers, and validators collectively vote. EIP-7594’s network-level analysis shows the probability of fooling a meaningful fraction of a large network falls extremely rapidly.

Erasure coding is essential here. Without it, an attacker might withhold only one crucial byte, making the original data unusable while giving random samplers almost no chance of selecting that byte. Erasure coding converts “a tiny important piece is missing” into “a large fraction of the encoded pieces must be unavailable.”

## Reconstruction and self-healing

A node that acquires at least half of all columns can reconstruct every blob and the missing columns. It can then redistribute the reconstructed columns to their corresponding subnets.

Thus PeerDAS is not merely checking storage: capable nodes and supernodes can actively repair gaps in the network’s distribution.

## What DAS does—and does not—guarantee

DAS provides high confidence that:

- the blob data committed to by the block was distributed;
- peers can retrieve enough authentic pieces to reconstruct it;
- a block producer cannot cheaply publish only commitments while hiding the underlying rollup data.

It does **not** mean:

- every node holds a complete copy;
- the rollup transactions are valid—fraud proofs, re-execution, or ZK proofs handle correctness;
- blob data remains retrievable forever.

Ethereum guarantees blob availability only for a protocol-defined retention window. Long-term historical storage is a separate **data retrievability** problem handled by rollup operators, archival services, or other storage networks.

## Current status

As of **October 24, 2026**, PeerDAS is live on Ethereum mainnet. It activated with the **Fusaka upgrade on December 3, 2025**. It is an intermediate step rather than “full Danksharding”: PeerDAS uses one-dimensional erasure coding within each blob, while future FullDAS designs envision more extensive two-dimensional coding and additional scaling.

In practical terms, PeerDAS lets Ethereum increase blob capacity for rollups without increasing every node’s bandwidth and storage proportionally—preserving the ability to run nodes on relatively ordinary hardware while giving L2s more data space.

answer:
Goldwasser–Micali encryption is **probabilistic because encryption uses fresh random coins**, so encrypting the same plaintext twice normally produces different ciphertexts.

For a single bit \(m\in\{0,1\}\), let the public key be \((N,z)\), where:

- \(N=pq\) is a product of secret primes;
- \(z\) is a quadratic nonresidue modulo \(N\) with Jacobi symbol \(+1\).

Encryption chooses a fresh uniform random \(r\in\mathbb Z_N^*\) and computes

\[
c=r^2z^m \pmod N.
\]

Thus:

- If \(m=0\), then \(c=r^2\) is a random quadratic residue.
- If \(m=1\), then \(c=r^2z\) is a random quadratic nonresidue of the appropriate type.

The random \(r\) means that each bit corresponds to an entire distribution of ciphertexts rather than one fixed ciphertext.

### Why randomness matters

If encryption were deterministic, an attacker possessing the public key could encrypt both possible bits and compare the results with the intercepted ciphertext. More generally, repeated plaintexts would produce repeated ciphertexts and leak equality patterns.

Randomization prevents that comparison: the attacker can generate encryptions of \(0\) or \(1\), but cannot expect any of them to equal the intercepted ciphertext. Distinguishing whether an intercepted value belongs to the residue or nonresidue distribution is assumed to be computationally hard—the **quadratic residuosity assumption**. The legitimate receiver, knowing \(p\) and \(q\), can determine the class and decrypt deterministically.

So “probabilistic” describes the **encryption operation**, not decryption: encryption has many possible outputs for a given message, while decryption still returns one definite bit. This construction was introduced as a way to achieve the modern notion of semantic security. [Goldwasser and Micali’s original paper](https://people.csail.mit.edu/silvio/Selected%20Scientific%20Papers/Encryption/Probabilistic_Encryption.pdf)

## Short answer

**PBFT trades openness for speed and deterministic finality; Nakamoto consensus trades speed and certainty for open participation and Sybil resistance.**

| Dimension | PBFT | Nakamoto consensus |
|---|---|---|
| Typical environment | Permissioned system with known replicas | Permissionless network with unknown participants |
| Decision mechanism | Authenticated quorum voting | Proof-of-work plus the valid chain with the most cumulative work |
| Fault threshold | Tolerates \(f\) Byzantine replicas with at least \(3f+1\) replicas | Security assumes attackers control less hash power than honest miners—simplified as below 50% |
| Finality | **Deterministic:** committed decisions do not revert under the assumptions | **Probabilistic:** deeper blocks become progressively harder, but never mathematically impossible, to reorganize |
| Normal operation | Primary proposes; replicas run pre-prepare, prepare, and commit phases | Miners independently compete to produce the next block; nodes validate it and follow the most-work valid chain |
| Communication | All-to-all voting produces roughly \(O(n^2)\) message traffic | Blocks and transactions are gossiped without an all-member voting round |
| Performance | Low latency and high throughput for a modest replica set | Higher latency; Bitcoin targets roughly ten-minute blocks and users may wait for multiple confirmations |
| Energy | No competitive hashing; mainly networking, signatures/MACs, and execution | Substantial proof-of-work computation and electricity |
| Network partition | Usually stops making progress if a quorum cannot communicate, preserving safety | Both sides may continue building chains; reconnection can discard the lower-work branch |
| Sybil resistance | External membership or identity system | Proof-of-work makes influence costly rather than assigning one vote per identity |
| Best suited to | Consortium ledgers, replicated databases, infrastructure services | Open cryptocurrencies and networks where validators cannot be preselected |

## How PBFT works

Classic PBFT is Byzantine-fault-tolerant **state-machine replication**:

1. A designated **primary** orders a client request.
2. It sends a **pre-prepare**.
3. Replicas exchange **prepare** messages.
4. They exchange **commit** messages.
5. After collecting a \(2f+1\) quorum, replicas execute the operation; the client accepts \(f+1\) matching replies.

With \(n=3f+1\), any two \(2f+1\) quorums overlap in enough replicas to include an honest one. This prevents two conflicting operations from both acquiring valid commit evidence. If the primary is faulty or unresponsive, replicas conduct a **view change** and select another primary. [Castro and Liskov describe the quorum sizes, phases, view changes, and linearizable safety property in detail.](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/Classes/739/Spring2004/Papers/p398-castro.pdf)

PBFT safety does not require messages to arrive within a known time: messages may be delayed, duplicated, lost, or reordered. **Liveness**, however, requires eventual weak synchrony—communication must eventually become timely enough to complete the protocol.

Its main scaling weakness is that the prepare and commit stages require replicas to multicast to one another. Consequently, adding validators rapidly increases communication and authentication work.

## How Nakamoto consensus works

“Nakamoto consensus” is the combination used by Bitcoin rather than a single explicit quorum vote:

1. Full nodes independently validate transactions and blocks.
2. Miners compete in a proof-of-work lottery.
3. A successful miner broadcasts a candidate block.
4. Other miners express acceptance by mining on top of it.
5. When branches compete, nodes select the **valid chain with the greatest cumulative proof of work**—often simplified as the “longest chain.”

Proof-of-work solves the open-membership problem: creating thousands of identities does not create thousands of votes because influence follows contributed hash power. Nakamoto described this as “one-CPU-one-vote,” although modern Bitcoin mining uses specialized hardware. [The original paper explains the proof-of-work mechanism, fork choice, incentives, and honest-hash-power assumption.](https://bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf)

Simultaneous blocks can create temporary forks. A later block normally makes one branch stronger, and nodes abandon the other. Thus, a transaction is not immediately final: every additional block makes reversal less probable, assuming honest miners retain the hash-power advantage. [Bitcoin’s developer guide describes these forks and selection of the most difficult chain to recreate.](https://developer.bitcoin.org/devguide/block_chain.html)

A hash-power majority does **not** automatically let an attacker create arbitrary coins, forge signatures, or make fully validating nodes accept invalid blocks. It can, however, reorganize recent valid history, double-spend the attacker’s own coins, censor transactions, or prevent confirmations.

## Fundamental trade-off

PBFT counts **identified replicas**, while Nakamoto consensus counts **scarce computational work**:

- PBFT asks: *Have at least \(2f+1\) authorized replicas explicitly agreed?*
- Nakamoto asks: *Which valid history has accumulated the most costly work?*

Therefore:

- Choose **PBFT** when the validator set is known and relatively small, and applications need fast, irreversible results.
- Choose **Nakamoto consensus** when anyone must be able to join without prior authorization and temporary forks plus probabilistic confirmation are acceptable.

answer:
**EIP-1559 separates the price of scarce block space from the payment to the block producer:** the protocol sets and burns a **base fee**, while users optionally pay a **priority fee** to incentivize a validator. This connects network congestion directly to ETH’s supply without eliminating validators’ incentive to include transactions.

### 1. Block-space pricing: a feedback mechanism

Ethereum measures computation in **gas**. Each block has a target gas usage and can temporarily use up to twice that target.

- If the previous block used **more than the target**, the next block’s base fee rises.
- If it used **less than the target**, the base fee falls.
- At the target, it remains unchanged.
- For execution gas, the adjustment ranges from −12.5% for an empty block to +12.5% for a full block.

Thus, temporary demand spikes can be absorbed by larger blocks, while sustained excess demand rapidly raises the price until some users wait or withdraw their transactions. This makes the base fee a protocol-computed reserve price rather than a price chosen by the validator. It improves predictability, but does **not necessarily make transactions cheaper**. [Ethereum’s gas documentation](https://ethereum.org/developers/docs/gas/) explains the current mechanism; the original specification is [EIP-1559](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1559).

For a type-2 transaction:

\[
\text{effective tip} =
\min(\text{maxPriorityFee},\ \text{maxFee}-\text{baseFee})
\]

\[
\text{actual payment}
=
\text{gas used}\times(\text{base fee}+\text{effective tip})
\]

Any unused portion of the user’s maximum fee is not paid.

### 2. Validator incentives: burn the rent, retain the marginal reward

The two fee components go to different places:

| Component | Determined by | Destination | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| Base fee | Protocol, from congestion | Burned | Prices scarce block space |
| Priority fee or tip | User | Block proposer/validator | Incentivizes inclusion and priority |
| Consensus reward | Proof-of-stake protocol | Validators | Pays for proposing, attesting and securing consensus |
| MEV | Transaction ordering/building | Proposer, builder and related parties | Additional ordering revenue |

Validators therefore maximize transaction-related income mainly through **tips and MEV**, not through the base fee. Consensus rewards are newly issued ETH, while tips and MEV normally redistribute existing ETH rather than create it. [Ethereum’s ether documentation](https://ethereum.org/developers/docs/intro-to-ether) distinguishes these sources.

Burning the base fee matters for incentives:

- If the proposer kept it, the proposer could more cheaply insert its own transactions, manufacture congestion, or arrange off-chain refunds.
- Because the base fee is destroyed, a proposer that submits fake transactions must actually bear that cost.
- Tips still give the proposer a reason to include useful transactions: a transaction paying only the base fee is valid, but produces no direct fee revenue for the proposer.

In economic terms, EIP-1559 assigns the **scarcity rent** from block space to the protocol-wide burn, while preserving a smaller marginal payment for the party doing the inclusion.

### 3. ETH supply: usage competes with issuance

For an individual block, the EIP-1559 burn is approximately:

\[
B_t = \text{base fee}_t \times \text{execution gas used}_t
\]

At the network level:

\[
\Delta \text{ETH supply}
=
\text{validator issuance}
-
\text{all ETH burned}
\]

Therefore:

- Low block-space demand → low base fees and little burning → issuance may exceed burn, producing net inflation.
- High demand → higher base fees and more gas consumed → burn may exceed issuance, producing net deflation over that period.
- Tips and MEV affect who owns ETH, but not total supply.
- EIP-1559 consequently does **not** establish a fixed supply or guarantee permanent deflation; the result depends on block-space demand relative to proof-of-stake issuance. [Ethereum’s issuance overview](https://ethereum.org/roadmap/merge/issuance/) describes this issuance-versus-burn balance.

A simple summary is:

> **Demand for Ethereum block space raises the protocol price; users pay that price in ETH; the protocol burns it; validators receive separate tips and issuance.**

As of October 24, 2026, this description concerns ordinary EVM execution gas. Blob data introduced by EIP-4844 has a separate, EIP-1559-like fee market and additional fee burning.

For an individual block, the EIP-1559 burn is approximately:

\[
B_t = \text{base fee}_t \times \text{execution gas used}_t
\]

At the network level:

\[
\Delta \text{ETH supply}
=
\text{validator issuance}
-
\text{all ETH burned}
\]

Therefore:

- Low block-space demand → low base fees and little burning → issuance may exceed burn, producing net inflation.
- High demand → higher base fees and more gas consumed → burn may exceed issuance, producing net deflation over that period.
- Tips and MEV affect who owns ETH, but not total supply.
- EIP-1559 consequently does **not** establish a fixed supply or guarantee permanent deflation; the result depends on block-space demand relative to proof-of-stake issuance. [Ethereum’s issuance overview](https://ethereum.org/roadmap/merge/issuance/) describes this issuance-versus-burn balance.

A simple summary is:

> **Demand for Ethereum block space raises the protocol price; users pay that price in ETH; the protocol burns it; validators receive separate tips and issuance.**

As of October 24, 2026, this description concerns ordinary EVM execution gas. Blob data introduced by EIP-4844 has a separate, EIP-1559-like fee market and additional fee burning.

Mozi’s “universal love” meant **impartial or inclusive concern for everyone**—Chinese *jiān’ài* (兼愛)—rather than equal emotional affection for every person. “Inclusive care” is therefore often a better translation.

Its central principle was:

> **Do not exclude someone’s welfare from moral consideration merely because that person belongs to another family, community, or state.**

Mozi connected this attitude with **mutual benefit**. People should treat others’ lives, families, property, and communities as matters worthy of protection, just as they protect their own. He believed narrow partiality caused society’s major evils: individuals injured others for personal advantage, families harmed other families, and states attacked other states. Inclusive concern would instead produce cooperation, assistance, peace, and social order. The *Mozi* therefore asks people to regard “other persons as one’s own person” and “other states as one’s own state.” [Chinese Text Project](https://ctext.org/mozi/book-4)

This did **not necessarily mean identical treatment**. Mohists continued to recognize particular duties toward parents, children, rulers, and neighbors. The important point was that strangers and outsiders must not be treated as morally worthless. In practice, universal care meant fulfilling one’s immediate responsibilities while refraining from harming outsiders, helping people in need, and supporting institutions that benefit everyone. Scholars consequently distinguish **equal moral concern** from **equal allocation of time, resources, or affection**. [Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/mohism/)

Mozi defended the doctrine in two main ways:

1. **Consequences:** inclusive concern promotes “benefit to the world,” whereas exclusion and partiality produce crime, oppression, and war.
2. **Heaven:** Mozi believed Heaven cares for and benefits everyone impartially, so human conduct should follow that model.

Thus, the simplest modern paraphrase is: **Act on the understanding that everyone’s welfare matters, not only your own or your group’s, and seek relationships and policies that benefit people mutually.** It resembles impartialist or consequentialist ethics more than the modern idea of feeling warm affection for all humanity. [Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy](https://iep.utm.edu/mozi/)

answer:
**Not universally.** A correctly designed commit–reveal protocol can stop **reactive front-running within a particular application**, but it does not eliminate every form of front-running or MEV on a public blockchain.

### How it works

1. **Commit:** Alice publishes an opaque commitment, such as  
   `H(action, parameters, beneficiary, randomSalt, contract, chainId)`.
2. The commitment becomes final or must age for a specified period.
3. **Reveal:** Alice publishes the action, parameters, and salt. The contract verifies that they match the earlier commitment and executes the action.

When an attacker first learns Alice’s action from the reveal, it is too late to create the required *older* commitment. ENS uses this approach for `.eth` registrations: the commitment must normally be between 60 seconds and 24 hours old before registration. [ENS documentation](https://docs.ens.domains/registry/eth/)

### Conditions required for it to work

The protocol must:

- Use a cryptographically random, sufficiently long salt; otherwise an attacker can guess low-entropy values from the commitment.
- Bind the commitment to the intended sender or beneficiary. Otherwise someone may copy the reveal, submit it with a higher fee, and claim the result.
- Include every security-relevant parameter, preferably along with the contract address and chain ID, to prevent alteration and cross-contract or cross-chain replay.
- Require a genuine separation between commit and reveal—such as different phases or a minimum commitment age—so a builder cannot insert a commitment and reveal ahead of the victim in the same block.
- Consume commitments once and impose sensible deadlines.
- Base priority or allocation on the commitment phase, rather than simply rewarding whichever reveal transaction executes first.

Ethereum’s commit-interface specification explicitly recommends strong salts, replay protection, one-time consumption, and appropriate time gaps. [ERC-5732](https://ercs.ethereum.org/ERCS/erc-5732)

### What it does **not** stop

- **Copying a badly bound reveal:** If the result goes to `msg.sender` and the prior commitment is not sender-bound, the revealed secret can still be stolen.
- **Speculative front-running:** Attackers can pre-commit many possible actions and reveal only the profitable one.
- **Selective non-reveal or last-revealer attacks:** In lotteries, voting, and randomness protocols, a participant may withhold its reveal after seeing others’ reveals.
- **Censorship and ordering among eligible reveals:** A block builder may delay reveals or reorder several already-valid commitments unless the protocol fixes or randomizes their order.
- **Information leakage:** The committing account, timing, value, gas use, and other metadata may disclose useful information; a weak salt or small action space may permit dictionary attacks.
- **Back-running:** Once the action executes publicly, searchers can trade on the resulting state.
- **External state manipulation:** If Alice commits through a wrapper but attackers can trade directly against the underlying AMM, they may see her reveal and change the AMM state before it executes. Commit–reveal works best when **all relevant competing actions are gated by the same commit phase**.

Even a 2026 Ethereum proposal specifically designed around transaction-level commit–reveal lists speculative front-running, back-running, withholding, metadata leakage, and extra delay as residual trade-offs. It remains a draft as of October 24, 2026. [EIP-8209](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-8209)

**Bottom line:** Commit–reveal is effective for things like name registration, sealed bids, and application-controlled contests when carefully implemented. It is a mitigation—not a general cure for public-mempool front-running—and continuous trading commonly needs additional mechanisms such as batch auctions, encrypted mempools, threshold encryption, private order flow, or protocol-enforced ordering. Academic analysis similarly finds that commit–reveal prevents the most severe reactive attacks under its model, but at the cost of two messages and delay. [Canidio and Danos](https://drops.dagstuhl.de/entities/document/10.4230/OASIcs.Tokenomics.2022.7)

Gríma kills Saruman because **years of domination, humiliation, and abuse finally push him past his breaking point**.

### In Tolkien’s book

The immediate trigger comes during **“The Scouring of the Shire.”** Frodo offers Gríma mercy and tells him that he does not have to follow Saruman. Saruman responds by publicly revealing that Gríma murdered Lotho Sackville-Baggins—on Saruman’s orders—then mocks and kicks him. Gríma finally snaps and cuts Saruman’s throat. [Tolkien Gateway](https://tolkiengateway.net/wiki/The_Scouring_of_the_Shire)

The deeper reasons are:

- Gríma has come to hate Saruman, despite remaining psychologically dependent on him.
- Saruman treats him as a contemptible tool, calling him “Worm” and repeatedly abusing him.
- Frodo’s offer of freedom briefly shows Gríma that escape is possible.
- Saruman’s final humiliation turns years of resentment into murderous rage.

So it is **not primarily an act of repentance or heroism**. It is a desperate act of revenge and rebellion by someone whom Saruman has thoroughly corrupted and degraded. Thematically, Saruman is destroyed by the same cruelty and contempt through which he tried to control others. [Tolkien Gateway](https://tolkiengateway.net/wiki/Gr%C3%ADma_Wormtongue)

### In Peter Jackson’s film

The extended edition moves the event from the Shire to Orthanc. Théoden offers Gríma freedom, but Saruman declares that Gríma will never be free and physically abuses him. Gríma then stabs Saruman in the back. It is essentially a compressed version of the book’s motivation: **mercy offers Gríma a way out, and Saruman’s final act of contempt makes him turn on his master**. The scene does not appear in the theatrical edition.

**The Aztec—more precisely, Mexica—state practiced human sacrifice for intertwined religious, political, and social reasons.** The strongest historical interpretation is not “religion *or* politics,” but that sacrifice made a sacred worldview and imperial power reinforce each other.

### Why was sacrifice practiced?

1. **Cosmic reciprocity and divine debt**  
   Mexica traditions held that gods had sacrificed themselves or shed their blood to create humanity, set the sun in motion, and sustain the present world. Humans therefore owed the gods a continuing “blood debt.” Offering blood, hearts, and life renewed divine energy and helped maintain the sun, rain, crops, and cosmic order. Sacrifice was understood as life-producing: death enabled regeneration rather than simply destroying life. Different festivals and gods required different victims and ceremonies; human sacrifice existed alongside animal offerings, food, valuables, and widespread ritual self-bloodletting. [Oxford Academic](https://academic.oup.com/book/481/chapter-abstract/135253092)

2. **Ritual re-enactment and embodiment**  
   Some victims served as *ixiptla*—living embodiments or representatives of a deity. Their treatment, costume, death, and sometimes the subsequent disposition of their bodies re-enacted creation myths and seasonal cycles. Thus victims were not always conceptualized merely as executed enemies, although that does not mean they freely consented.

3. **War, status, and imperial legitimacy**  
   Many victims were captured warriors. Presenting captives at the Templo Mayor turned military victory into visible evidence that the ruler, army, priesthood, and patron god Huitzilopochtli possessed divine favor. Capturing enemies also brought individual warriors promotion and prestige. Public ceremonies helped unite the ruling and warrior classes, affirmed the ruler’s role as intermediary with the gods, and displayed power to allies, rivals, and tributary communities. Archaeologists consequently treat state religion not simply as private belief but as part of how Mexica authority was organized and justified. [Cambridge Archaeological Journal](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/cambridge-archaeological-journal/article/abs/huitzilopochtlis-conquest-aztec-ideology-in-the-archaeological-record/BB5ED1B0E988FE712D62DBE6636B7A42)

These functions should not be separated too sharply. Mexica rulers could sincerely believe sacrifice was cosmically necessary **and** use it to legitimate conquest. Religion was not merely cynical propaganda pasted onto an otherwise secular state.

### What do historians dispute?

**1. The scale—not the basic existence—of sacrifice.**  
Human sacrifice is archaeologically confirmed. The Templo Mayor precinct has yielded ritually modified human remains, sacrificial equipment, and the *Huei Tzompantli*, including hundreds of skulls with preparation and display marks. Recent INAH study of the skull tower also confirms that victims included women and children as well as adult men. [INAH](https://www.inah.gob.mx/boletines/a-10-anos-del-hallazgo-del-huei-tzompantli-de-tenochtitlan-los-craneos-humanos-son-objeto-de-analisis-de-vanguardia)

What cannot be securely calculated is the annual death toll. Early colonial texts offer wildly varying figures. The famous claim that **80,400 people were killed during the 1487 dedication of the Templo Mayor in four days** presents severe logistical problems. Claims of 20,000 or more victims every year are also based on uncertain, sometimes untraceable or polemical colonial reports. Archaeology confirms substantial and repeated killing but cannot yet convert excavated remains into a reliable yearly total. One scholarly reconstruction found roughly 500 victims identifiable in an annual ritual calendar, while suggesting that a figure in the low thousands might be possible once exceptional ceremonies are included—but even that is an estimate, not a consensus. [Caroline Dodds Pennock’s assessment](https://eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/98071/1/2_PDFsam_ssoar-hsr-2012-3-dodds_pennock-Mass_murder_or_religious_homicide.pdf)

**2. How much weight to give religion versus state power.**  
Some interpretations foreground sincere beliefs about divine sustenance, cosmic debt, fertility, and regeneration. Others emphasize intimidation, political integration, elite cohesion, and the conversion of conquered bodies into symbols of imperial authority. Most historians now regard these as mutually reinforcing rather than exclusive explanations, but they disagree over which was primary and how ordinary people understood state ideology.

**3. Whether warfare was organized chiefly to obtain victims.**
